The Debut is a movie that blends comedy, horror and drama so effectively it’s impossible to define it as one. And it's a movie that does so by showcasing one of the most incredible, and endearing, acting tour-de-forces of a lifetime from Julianne Moore.
Jesse Eisenberg directed film starring Julianne Moore is a tour de force

Every year, there are Oscar-bait films: stories designed to play on the emotions and sentimentalities of a voting body that seem to care more about how artistic a movie feels than actually is. And every year, audiences turn against them as contrived, out of touch and desperate.

Which you'd think could bode poorly for Julianne Moore, star of writer-director Jesse Eisenberg's The Debut — at least when it comes to how regular audiences might feel about a performance best described as "psychotically genius."

Because on its face, the chaotic, carnivalesque community theatre parable presents with all the risk factors: entertainment about the world of entertainment, absurdist high-minded comedy that feels straight out of a New Yorker cartoon, and a main character that reads like a cross between Patti LuPone in Evita and Joaquin Phoenix in Joker.

In short, it's the kind of thing that might feel designed in a lab to win an Oscar — and therefore, come off as annoyingly self-important to actual audiences when they get to see it. But on that front, there are two bits of good news for The Debut. The first is that this thing is almost definitely going to nab that Oscar. And the second is that it won’t do it by being disingenuous.

Because this is quite clearly one of the most shatteringly good movies of the year; a film that blends comedy, horror and drama so effectively it’s impossible to define it as any one genre. And it's a movie that does so by showcasing one of the most incredible, and endearing, acting tour-de-forces of a lifetime.

The Debut is anchored by Moore's stunning, unrestrained performance as Mona — despite, initially, seeming as shallow as it gets. A demure housewife with two near-adult children and emotionally immature husband, Mona apparently hasn’t been given the privilege of developing an interior life. Instead, she seems to have spent the past 50 or so years in the painfully simple, almost fableistic role constructed around her.

She makes dinner for an unappreciative family in a house that looks like it was decorated by a cross between Martha Stewart and Doctor Seuss. She goes to weekly cocktail nights with a couple who don't even pretend to hear her speak. And when she talks, she does so in a quiet, plain, sing-song voice that practically screams "please don’t be mad at me." Not that she has the confidence to scream about anything, to anyone at all.

That is, until she decides to audition for a community theatre production of Nosy Neighbors — a fictional musical about all the zany inhabitants of a seedy apartment building, in which she would play building super Ms. Danielle.

It's an obviously good-spirited takedown of plays in the style of 7 Stories and The Dining Room —the ensemble-based, zany-characters-share-a-single-location-type of stories that tend to clog up community theatre calendars. It's a refreshing specificity only someone familiar with community theatre would know: the perennial struggle to find plays with enough jokes to go around for everyone auditioning.

That is Eisenberg to a tee. Having done community theatre from six years old, he's spoken about his love for the types of people you encounter there often, and worked on it, too: his 2019 off-Broadway play Happy Talk cast Susan Sarandon as a musical-worshipping suburban housewife, slavishly obsessed with her role in a rinky-dink staging of South Pacific. Like Mona, she is a woman who talks incessantly about her star turn as if she's Liza Minnelli in Cabaret, though to a husband — and by extension, world — that refuses to notice.

The self-evidently pathetic tragedy of a woman scrambling for meaning and recognition universally denied her is the exact same theme returned to in The Debut. Because as Mona blithers on about her own upcoming role, there’s only one problem: she’s terrible. Comically terrible. Cosmically, incomparably bad in a way that increasingly suggests there's something deeper, more disturbing wrong with her.

items: Apple TV's Mayday is propaganda — and it rocks
Ridley Scott's The Dog Stars bombs at the box office. Here's what that tells us about what audiences want

blocks.text: It's a problem that at first, washed-up, big-fish-little-pond director Jerry (Paul Giamatti) feels he can coach out of her. The bizarre trajectory that follows is better seen than read about, though it's an obvious homage to films centred on delusional, self-obsessed characters like The King of Comedy, Taxi Driver and, yes, Joker give Moore an infinitely fertile playground to do things most actors only dream of.

And it is all done as her character seeks to find truth in fiction at literally any cost, like a more-than-half-crazed Uta Hagen — the iconic teacher who influenced a generation of actors to invent and know nearly every aspect of their entire character's life. Even if they only delivered one line.

It is an approach Mona, who starts with no life of her own, takes to the most terrifying conclusion. The kaleidoscopic, astonishing, horribly hilarious journey it takes her on is not quite of the laugh-until-you-cry variety; it's maybe closer to cry-until-you-laugh. Or maybe do both simultaneously until you forget what you were feeling in the first place.
Absent inner life

Here, Moore portrays a woman whose inner life and self-worth was so completely strangled they appeared to have atrophied into nothing. And then that burst forward with such propellant, stunning force you are nearly blinded by looking at the screen.

It’s largely accomplished by Eisenberg's tightly efficient, but confidently assured writing, which is both effectively engineered and feels so loose it seems nearly like improvisation; we are given just enough hints at Mona’s backstory without being spoonfed, and allowed to draw our own ludicrous conclusions.

The supporting cast is also uniquely excellent; alongside the heartbreakingly effective two-hander between Giamatti (channelling the tough-mentor success of The Holdovers) and Moore, the Nosy Neighbors cast and crew more than hold her own. Halle Bailey's casting as the play's lead lets her showcase her pipes and acting palette. While up-and-comer Eldar Isgandarov, playing easily-cowed assistant Piotr, flexes the comedic muscles he also shows off in the equally incredible Club Kid, which is also playing at TIFF.
Film industry has built 'solid bridge' between Canada and U.S., says TIFF CEO
But again, this is Moore’s show — one where she expands the cliche, male-dominated archetype of unhinged, at-the-fringes desperado with aplomb.

The result is an acting performance for the ages. A chameleonic cycle of transformations that should, and will, go down in the history books. And one that situates her in a uniquely comfortable position when it comes to the Oscars race. Because Moore in The Debut is something to behold, and seems impossible to ignore.
And most importantly, it all seems genuine.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Germany: CDU ahead in Lower Saxony local election
articles.summary: The CDU is on course to win in municipal polls in the northwestern state of Lower Saxony that were seen as a gauge of support for the far-right AfD party. DW has more.
articles.byline: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez, Timothy Jones, Karl Sexton, Mark Hallam, Emilio Reynoso, Richard Connor, Dmytro Hubenko

image.caption: Voters in Lower Saxony chose mayors, district administrators and councilsImage: Hauke-Christian Dittrich/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 13, 2026
CDU ahead in Lower Saxony municipal elections, projection says

Municipal elections in Lower Saxony provided a sigh of relief to the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), currently in the spotlight in the wake of gains by the far-right AfD in the state of Saxony-Anhalt regional elections last week.
According to a projection by Infratest dimap published by German broadcaster NDR, the CDU held 27.7% of the vote, ahead of the SPD at 24.5% and the AfD, with 16.5%.
The Greens came in fourth with 13.6%, followed by The Left at 5.9% and the FDP 3.6%.
CDU state leader Sebastian Lechner was optimistic hours before the projections were released, saying the CDU could buck the national trend in Lower Saxony.

"As you know, these local elections did not exactly take place under easy circumstances. We, too, have noticed the discontent over Berlin," Lechner said, acknowledging that his party had a "credibility problem" that should be addressed.

The results in Lower Saxony was being closely watched by Chancellor Merz, especially as his CDU is expected to face a debacle next Sunday in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where support for the party recently plummeted to 7% in polls

blocks.text: Published September 14, 2026 8:07am
Transport group Manibela on Monday began its two-day nationwide transport strike against rising fuel prices with members gathering in Quezon City.

As of early Monday morning, the situation remained normal on several major roads in Manila as many jeepneys were still operating and commuters were able to get rides, according to Super Radyo dzBB's Pamela Adriano.

NORMAL PA RIN SA GITNA NG PAGKILOSSitwasyon sa lungsod ng Maynila, nananatiling normal sa kabila ng ikinasang tigil–pasada ng grupong MANIBELA ngayong araw. | via @PamelaAdriano pic.twitter.com/jdnMHHMXml— DZBB Super Radyo (@dzbb) September 13, 2026
Jeepneys were still plying routes along España Boulevard, including trips to Quiapo and Claro M. Recto Avenue, as well as Buendia, Vito Cruz, Libertad, and Taft Avenue routes.
Several universities in Manila, including the University of Santo Tomas, Far Eastern University, and Adamson University, also announced the suspension of face-to-face classes due to the strike.
Manibela members started gathering at Philcoa along Commonwealth Avenue in Quezon City for the protest action, according to a report of Super Radyo dzBB's Allan Gatus.

PAGKILOS NG GRUPONG MANIBELAIlang miyembro ng grupong MANIBELA, nagsimula nang magtipon-tipon sa PHILCOA–Commonwealth Avenue sa Quezon City. | via @allangatus pic.twitter.com/jFWoO3t56q— DZBB Super Radyo (@dzbb) September 13, 2026
They said rising fuel prices were affecting drivers' earnings. The group said the continuing increase in fuel costs was forcing drivers to spend a large portion of their daily earnings on fuel.
Manibela earlier said the net increase in fuel prices since January, as of August 31, already reached P54.92 per liter for gasoline and P59.06 per liter for diesel.

The group is calling for concrete measures to ease the burden of high fuel costs, such as the suspension of petroleum taxes, more accessible fuel subsidy programs, and a review of existing policies governing the country's oil industry.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Article II starts: Unexplained wealth charge, P6.77-B record at Duterte trial
articles.summary: Bank records, SALNs and tax documents take center stage Monday.

blocks.text: September 14, 2026 | 7:47am
MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte's trial is set to shift to the paper trail behind her alleged unexplained wealth, covered under Article II of her four impeachment charges.
House prosecutors are expected to begin presenting evidence for allegations that her assets and financial interests do not square with her lawful income and official wealth declarations.

The Senate impeachment court is set to resume at 10 a.m. on Monday, September 14 with the unexplained wealth charge, after prosecutors last week ended their presentation of witnesses for the confidential funds article.

Bank, tax, corporate and other financial records obtained through subpoenas from the impeachment court will be tackled. Considered a smoking gun is the Anti-Money Laundering Council report covering billions of pesos in transactions involving Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.
More than 1,800 documents, including bank and insurance records, were set aside for marking last week in preparation for Article II.

Rep. Chel Diokno (Akbayan party-list), one of the prosecutors handling the article, has also served Duterte's defense with 104 requests for admission aimed at establishing the authenticity of financial records and ownership of bank accounts without requiring witnesses to authenticate each document.
But the prosecution will ultimately have to establish more than the movement of large sums through bank accounts.
P6.77 billion in cash flows

The AMLC told the House justice committee in April that banks had filed 630 covered transaction reports and 33 suspicious transaction reports involving Duterte and Carpio from 2006 to 2025, with the transactions totaling P6.77 billion.
Of the total, P3.77 billion was attributed to Duterte and P2.99 billion to Carpio.
AMLC figures presented during the House proceedings put roughly P4.4 billion in inflows and P1.5 billion in outflows, while about P791 million could not be classified as either.

The P6.77-billion figure is an aggregate of transactions recorded over nearly two decades. It does not mean Duterte and Carpio held P6.77 billion at any one time, nor does the figure by itself establish unexplained wealth.

Covered transaction reports are generated when transactions meet statutory reporting thresholds and do not necessarily indicate suspicious activity. Suspicious transaction reports, by contrast, involve transactions flagged by covered institutions based on circumstances defined under anti-money laundering laws.
The prosecution will therefore have to connect the financial activity in the records to Duterte's declared assets, lawful sources of income and business interests.
SALNs against financial records
During the House impeachment proceedings, lawmakers focused on what they described as a mismatch between Duterte's bank activity and her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.

Records submitted by the Office of the Ombudsman showed that Duterte declared no cash on hand or bank deposits from 2019 to 2024, while her declared net worth increased from P55.6 million to P88.5 million during the same period.
Duterte has disputed the prosecution's interpretation of the records.

Defense lawyer Michael Poa previously stressed that the AMLC figures represent aggregated deposits, withdrawals and other transactions over many years and should not be treated as the amount of money Duterte and Carpio possessed.
Poa has also said Duterte's cash was included under the "others" category of her SALN rather than separately declared as cash on hand or in banks.
Duterte has maintained that she declared her assets and money in her SALNs and that her wealth came from legitimate and documented sources.

The impeachment court in July ordered the production of peso-denominated bank records, AMLC reports and relevant tax records involving Duterte, Carpio and entities linked to them after finding the requested documents prima facie relevant to Article II.

Presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero, however, imposed a significant limitation on historical records from 2007 to 2021: they may be used only as a comparative financial baseline for Duterte's current term and not to establish separate impeachable offenses from earlier periods.
Who may testify

The prosecution has asked the impeachment court to subpoena retired Sandiganbayan justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang, Office of the Ombudsman records officer Karen Batu and Securities and Exchange Commission official Gerard Del Rosario as witnesses for Article II.
Prosecutors said Cabotaje-Tang would testify on principles governing public accountability, unexplained wealth and prohibited business interests.

Batu is expected to identify and authenticate SALNs and other relevant Ombudsman records, while Del Rosario is expected to authenticate corporate records involving ownership, positions and business interests.
Officials from the AMLC, Bureau of Internal Revenue, banks and other institutions are also among the potential witnesses as prosecutors build the documentary chain behind the financial records.

The prosecution has said it is considering around 25 witnesses for Article II, although the number could be reduced if the defense admits the authenticity or ownership of documents covered by its requests for admission.
The impeachment court gave Duterte's lawyers 15 days to respond to the 104 requests.
Monday begins another three-day stretch of morning impeachment sessions from September 14 to 16, followed by a regular plenary session.

On Wednesday, the court is also expected to hear four amici curiae, or friends of the court, on a separate issue that could determine the threshold for conviction: how the constitutional two-thirds requirement should be computed when some senator-judges are unable to participate.

articles.title: One Nation vows to cut migration by 750,000 sparking fears for key industries including aged care
articles.summary: New immigration policy has attracted bipartisan condemnation with Labor warning it would damage construction, aged care and agriculture

blocks.text: One Nation says it will cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years, targeting international students and the family members of skilled migrants in a “net-negative” plan.
But Labor has said it would cause sweeping damage to construction, health care, aged care and disability sectors, and the Liberals have cast doubt about whether any modelling underpinned the figure.
The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, said the new policy, announced on Monday, would “reset” Australia’s immigration system and help ease pressure on housing and public services.

Temporary visa numbers would be returned to 2017 levels, under what Hanson says would represent a net-negative arrivals rate for the first three years. That would mean the net overseas migration (Nom) total would be 130,000 under the One Nation plan.

The announcement comes as both Labor and the Coalition consider new cuts to overseas arrivals, in an increasingly charged contest ahead of the next federal election. Hanson will hope her plan plays well ahead of the Victorian state election, due in November.
“I know Australians are doing it tough,” Hanson said in a statement.

“Families are competing with hundreds of people for rental accommodation. Patients are stuck in ambulances because there are not enough hospital beds. Young Australians are being locked out of home ownership while wages and infrastructure fail to keep up.”

The policy also drive division within One Nation, with lower house MP David Farley previously expressing concern that big cuts to immigration could deny his electorate of Farrer the workers needed to care for elderly people and work on farms.
Hanson said One Nation would give “illegal migrants” three months to leave, with those who depart voluntarily given the ability to apply for visas in the future.
“Those who remain unlawfully after this period will be subject to immigration enforcement and a lifetime ban from re-entering Australia,” she said.
The Pacific labour mobility (Palm) scheme for agriculture would remain in place under One Nation’s plan, but temporary skilled migrants would lose the ability to apply for visas for family members.
“We will take back control of who comes here and how many we accept, train more Australians, restore living standards and put the safety and security of Australians first.”

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, have held talks on Labor’s delayed migration package in recent days. It is expected to further drive down net overseas migration.
after newsletter promotion
But Labor has struggled to finalise the plan and delayed its announcement by more than a month.
The deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, told News24 Hanson had plucked the number out of nowhere and has no modelling to back it up.
“Simply saying we’re going to have negative migration for a number of years, negative Nom, well, that would be a real shock to the economy, and it would make all Australians poorer,” she said.
“It’s so important to get this right, because sending the country into recession means that all Australians pay the price. It simply can’t be a slogan, you have to do the work behind it.”
The health minister, Mark Butler, warned One Nation’s cuts would kill critical industries.
“Pauline Hanson said a few weeks ago, she didn’t care what the impact of her migration policy would be on business, but this is just another level entirely.
“This is going to smash industries like construction. It would devastate the health sector and aged care and disability.”

articles.title: Around 800 teachers withdraw from BARMM poll duties
articles.summary: Hundreds of teachers sought exemption from election assignments.

blocks.text: September 14, 2026 | 7:17am

Cops guard a stretch of thoroughdffare thoroughfare in Cotabato City as part of the security efforts meant to ensure safe and fraud-free Bangsamoro parliamentary elections in all of its 37 barangays on Monday, Sept. 14, 2026.
Philstar.com / John Unson

COTABATO CITY — Apprehensive of possible hostilities, 839 teachers in the Bangsamoro region have reportedly withdrawn from their September 14 election duties in polling places in areas with security concerns.

Catholic radio station DXMS in Cotabato City reported Sunday that Commission on Elections Chairman George Erwin Garcia confirmed that teachers who withdrew from election duties were based in Lanao del Sur, Tawi-Tawi and Maguindanao del Sur, the Bangsamoro Special Geographic Area and Cotabato City.
The Bangsamoro Special Geographic Area has eight municipalities formed from 63 former barangays of Cotabato province that voted to join the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.

DXMS, one of six radio stations in Central Mindanao operated by the Catholic Notre Dame Broadcasting Corporation, also reported that 137 teachers in different schools in Cotabato City had asked election officials to excuse them from their poll assignments.

BARMM covers the provinces of Maguindanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Lanao del Sur, Basilan and Tawi-Tawi, as well as the cities of Lamitan, Marawi and Cotabato. Its regional government center is in Cotabato City.

Some towns in Maguindanao del Sur and Lanao del Sur include communities of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front and are also affected by violent clan feuds involving armed groups, some of which are reportedly supporting rival aspirants for seats in the 80-member Bangsamoro Parliament.

Maj. Gen. Jose Vladimir Cagara, acting commander of the military's Western Mindanao Command; Brig. Gen. Ricky Bunayog, acting commander of the Army's 6th Infantry Division; and Police Brig. Gen. Christopher Abecia, director of the Police Regional Office-Bangsamoro Autonomous Region, have separately assured the public that their units are prepared to secure polling sites across BARMM.

articles.title: Missing US hiker, 70, found injured on remote island after week-long search
articles.summary:
Craig Berg was hypothermic but alert when located on Isle Royale by Michigan police and officials during solo hike

A 70-year-old hiker who had been missing for a week on a

blocks.text: A 70-year-old hiker who had been missing for a week on a Michigan island was rescued on Saturday, according to the US Coast Guard.

Craig Berg was located on Isle Royale with the help of backpackers, Michigan state police troopers and local officials. Even though Berg was found injured and hypothermic, he is “alive and alert”, according to a statement posted to the Isle Royale national park’s Facebook page.

After Berg was located, a MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from US Coast Guard Air Station Traverse City hoisted Berg from the island and transported him to Marquette regional airport in Gwinn, Michigan, 140 miles (230km) away.
The Isle Royale national park’s statement reported that Berg had been missing since 5 September.

Berg was on what was planned as a nine-day solo backpacking hike on the large Lake Superior island. He was supposed to take a ferry back to Michigan’s Upper Peninsula on 5 September, but family members said that he did not arrive home.
According to Local 4, a Detroit station, Berg’s family reported him missing when the hiker did not return as planned. Search and rescue missions began on 6 September.

Crews first focused on Rock Harbor, where Berg planned to end his hike, then expanded to other areas – including the Greenstone Ridge trail, where a trail camera captured Berg on 30 August, the report added.
In an interview with TV6, Berg’s son, Evan, said that he is happy and relieved that his father has been located.

“He was in rough shape, but he’s okay,” Evan said. “He’s able to speak. He asked for food and water. We’re just so grateful, and we couldn’t be more happy and relieved, and we appreciate all the support we’ve had on social media, and we are just so grateful.”
The National Park Service thanks the employees and partners who helped during the search.

​Isle Royale is a remote national park with no roads or wheeled vehicles allowed. Ground search teams navigating the island’s 200 sq miles of solid land must move strictly by foot through dense boreal forest and rocky ridges.
Berg’s rescue brings a successful conclusion to an intensive, week-long multi-agency operation across the remote, roadless island.

articles.title: Sweden election 'very close' as left bloc claims tight lead
articles.summary: The left-wing opposition is narrowly ahead, but it will be "very close," Social Democrat leader Andersson said.

image.caption: Andersson's leftist bloc has a narrow lead going into the tight raceImage: Denis Balibouse/REUTERS

blocks.text: Sweden's election was too close to call after more than 86% of ballots had been counted on Sunday night.

Former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson, whose Social Democrats lead a left-wing opposition coalition and is hoping to return to power after four years, said early on Monday morning that "it looks like it will be very close."
"We Social Democrats will always be ready to assume responsibility for the result... For now, we are in the lead. And if that is confirmed, Sweden will have a new government," she told supporters.

Incumbent Ulf Kristersson, who leads a right-wing alliance that includes the far-right Sweden Democrats, said he would reach out to other party leaders for discussions, and that it was unclear who would be governing the country in the coming years.

"The voters have had their say, but we still don't have a final result. Which government will lead Sweden in the coming years is still an open question, and we will do everything we can to ensure that this government will be the very best for our country," Kristersson said.
A victory by the right-wing bloc would bring the far-right Sweden Democrats into government for the first time.
Leftist bloc sees pre-poll lead cut as election neared
Ahead of the election, opinion polls had predicted an easy win for the left-wing alliance over the right-wing group led by incumbent Kristersson.
But the four-party opposition alliance had seen that lead narrow as election day approached.

"We all knew it was going to be a very close election; I've said that all along," Andersson, the first woman to serve as Swedish Prime Minister in 2021-2022, told a rally in the Swedish capital Saturday.
"Now it's up to voters: do they want a government that will be totally dominated by the Sweden Democrats, or do they want a government led by me?"

blocks.caption: Kristersson's right-wing group has surged in the polls in recent weeksImage: Pontus Lundahl/TT Nyhetsbyrån/picture alliance

blocks.text: What do we know about the main parties in Sweden's election?
The Social Democrats have governed in Sweden for most of the last century and remain the country's largest party.
The left-wing bloc has promised to boost the welfare state and address rising costs.
Kristersson's campaign has focused on his government's record of reducing violent and organized crime and clamping down on immigration.

A victory at the ballot box on Sunday would suggest voters approve of that approach, supporters of the right-wing bloc say. Critics have denounced the agenda as undermining civil liberties and unfairly targeting immigrants.
"We can unify parties, voters and issues into joint action. That's why ​we get things ‌done," Kristersson said this week in parliament.
Sweden's youth crime: Are tougher laws the answer?
Far right could enter government for first time

Unlike in Germany, where most parties have ruled out working with the far-right Alternative for Germany as part of the political "firewall", Kristersson has promised the Sweden Democrats key government posts if his alliance wins.

The leader of the far-right party, Jimmie Akesson, told a campaign rally in Stockholm on Saturday that the Sweden Democrats "have already won," as the party eyes power for the first time since entering parliament in 2010.
"Sweden is becoming safer, better, and more Swedish," the 47-year-old said.

blocks.caption: Some of the founders of Akesson's party had ties to Sweden's neo-Nazi movementImage: Magnus Lejhall/TT News Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Akesson is expected to be given the role of migration minister if the right-wing alliance wins on Sunday.
Eight million people are eligible to vote in a country of 10.6 million people. Turnout regularly exceeds 80% in Sweden.
Polling stations close at 8 p.m. (1900 UTC). The first results will be expected several hours later on Sunday night.
Around half of the votes have already been cast in advance.

articles.title: Hidden history of royal staff uncovered in Buckingham Palace restoration
articles.summary:
Whist drive ticket embedded in rock and news article on Great Train Robbers among items discovered during 10-year restoration

Lost or long-discarded items revealing glimpses of the…

blocks.text: Lost or long-discarded items revealing glimpses of the behind-the-scenes life of Buckingham Palace staff over decades have been uncovered during the restoration of the UK monarchy’s HQ.

Misplaced belongings, found beneath the floorboards, in other areas of the royal residence and preserved within the fabric of the building, include a ticket to a whist drive run by the royal household’s social club from nearly 80 years ago.

Blank Littlewoods football pools betting slips from 1957, a pair of battered black hobnail boots and an empty Silk Cut cigarette packet were among the everyday objects unearthed, as well as an almost 140-year-old fragment of the West End theatre listings from the Standard newspaper in 1889.

The discoveries were made during the decade-long £370m reservicing of the palace which has included rewiring electrics, upgrading plumbing and heating and overhauling its infrastructure to prevent long-term damage.

blocks.caption: About 1.2 miles of Vulcanised Indian Rubber cabling was discovered and removed as a priority.  Photograph: Aaron Chown/PA

blocks.text: Electrical wire covered with Vulcanised Indian Rubber (VIR) cabling, which posed the risk of fire to the building, were also located. The cabling, which becomes brittle with age, was removed as a priority when the project, which is due to be completed next year, began in 2017. About 1.2 miles (2km) of the rubber cabling has been replaced so far.

blocks.caption: The ticket to the whist drive organised by the staff social club, dated 14 April 1949, was embedded in a lump of rock. Photograph: Aaron Chown/PA

blocks.text: The small whist drive ticket, priced at 6d, a sixpence, and dated 14 April 1949 – during the reign of the king’s grandfather, George VI – was found embedded in a lump of building rock.
The pass to the staff social club gathering in the palace reads “Royal Household Social Club – Buckingham Palace: A Whist Drive to be held on” followed by the faded, stamped date “14 APR 1949”.
At that time, Queen Elizabeth II was still Princess Elizabeth and had been married to Prince Philip for less than 18 months and their eldest son, Charles, was only five months old.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Pages from the Daily Express in 1966 detailing the prison housing the Great Train Robbers. Photograph: Aaron Chown/PA

blocks.text: Pages from the Daily Express newspaper in 1966 detailed the maximum security prison housing the Great Train Robbers, picturing the inside of Durham prison and reporting that “the men who were found guilty of stealing a fortune in mailbags spend their week stitching them for nine shillings”.

blocks.caption: Instructions for royal household staff for the 1977 Silver Jubilee Diplomatic Corps reception. Photograph: Aaron Chown/PA

blocks.text: Instructions for royal household staff for the 1977 Silver Jubilee Diplomatic Corps reception informed them that the queen and other members of the royal family would move round the ballroom in a “clockwise direction”.

Aides were to encourage the 350 British guests to mingle with the diplomats at the glittering white tie and tiaras annual gathering, according to the manually typed sheet, which also said that smoking was banned in the certain state rooms and the reception kept to a strict timetable.

Other findings included a section of Minton decorative ceramic tiles from a fireplace hearth, with the design dating from around the mid-1800s, an aged Pewter tankard, a bottle of Schweppes still Malvern English spring water, a wooden junction box and a faded box containing six Christmas cards.

articles.title: Early results have Swedish centre-left with 1-seat lead over rivals in general election
articles.summary: Sweden's national election results showed a dead heat on Sunday, with a partial count by the election authority indicating a ‌one-seat majority for the opposition centre-left bloc that could halt the…

image.caption: A voter casts a ballot at a polling station in Malmo, Sweden, on Sunday. (Johan Nilsson/TT News Agency/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Sweden's national election results showed a dead heat on Sunday, with a partial count by the election authority indicating a ‌one-seat majority for the opposition centre-left bloc that could halt the Nordic nation's drift away from its liberal heritage.
PM vows to bring far-right party into his conservative coalition if they win re-election

The bloc, headed by the Social Democrats' party leader Magdalena Andersson, was expected to win 175 seats in the 349-seat parliament, the Riksdag, based on votes from 4,853 of Sweden's 6,312 election districts, the election authority said.
The right-wing governing bloc of Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson was seen winning ​174 seats, with ballot-counting continuing.
The election, while unlikely to change the course of Sweden's pro-Western ​and pro-Ukraine stance, will decide whether Kristersson's push toward a hard-right clampdown on migration continues.
Given the closeness of the race, the winner may not be known for several days, after all overseas ballots have been counted.

In a pre-election pledge, Kristersson ​broke a longstanding taboo and said he would bring into government the Sweden Democrats, a far-right party with roots in ⁠the Nazi fringe, as he aims to ⁠create a majority-right coalition.
Many voters on the right say a win would ‌amount to an endorsement of policies that have helped to curb gang violence and cut immigration dramatically.

items: Swedish election could see far-right party join government for 1st time

blocks.text: But some Swedes have expressed wariness, saying Kristersson's invitation to the far right was a step too far.

"I think it will be a long night," said Maria Malmer Stenergard, Minister for Foreign Affairs and a member of Kristersson's Moderate Party. "Maybe we won't even have the results until Wednesday when the ⁠votes that have been cast abroad arrive."
Kristersson, who has trailed in opinion polls throughout his four years in office, had been catching up in the final weeks of campaigning, with Andersson and her Social Democrats losing ground.

Critics say the Kristersson government's immigration policies, whose incentives and penalties press migrants either to conform more closely to ‌Swedish cultural norms or leave the country, are undermining civil liberties.

Electoral success for the Sweden Democrats would be welcomed by Europe's ascendant far-right parties, which were bolstered by the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany's win in a German state election last week.

items: Far-right victory in German state expected to send shockwaves throughout the world

blocks.text: The far right hopes for gains in upcoming elections across Europe, with the National Rally's bid for the French presidency next year potentially its biggest prize.

While voting on Saturday in Rinkeby, near Stockholm, the Sweden Democrats' longstanding leader Jimmie Akesson said the suburb, home to one of the country's biggest Swedish-Somali populations, "doesn't look like Sweden."

Sweden was long one of ⁠Europe's most welcoming countries for immigrants until Kristersson came to power four years ago. His government abolished permanent residency for refugees, tightened welfare rules and stepped ⁠up expulsions of those without a right to stay.

The Sweden Democrats acknowledge that their party was founded in part by neo-Nazis and white ⁠supremacists in ⁠the 1980s, but say they have eliminated such extremists from ​their ranks and have apologized for their past.

Cheers broke out at the Sweden Democrats' election party after an updated projection from Swedish broadcaster SVT showed a much ​narrower gap than an initial exit poll, ⁠which had put the centre-left opposition ahead with 51 per cent of the vote.

"You cannot imagine how nervous I am right now. It feels like my life's work is hanging in the balance," said Ludvig Aspling, a member of parliament and immigration spokesperson for the Sweden Democrats. "It is going to be super tight. We still have a chance."

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 24: What to expect
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court on Monday will begin tackling Article 2 of the impeachment case, which accuses Vice President Sara Duterte of accumulating unexplained wealth.

blocks.text: Published September 14, 2026 6:11am
The Senate impeachment court on Monday will begin tackling Article 2 of the impeachment case, which accuses Vice President Sara Duterte of accumulating unexplained wealth.
Former Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang will be the first witness that the House prosecution panel will call, according to impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol.
He said the prosecution will seek to qualify Cabotaje-Tang as an expert witness in the trial.

“‘Pag expert witness po para po siyang in a way parang amici, amicus curiae na sasabihin niya kung paano ‘yung proseso ng isang hukom para ma-determine kung meron bang unexplained wealth o improperly accumulated wealth ‘yung isang opisyales,” Tongol told Senate reporters last Friday.

(An expert witness acts, in a way, like an amicus curiae (friend of the court). She would explain the process a judge follows to determine whether an official possesses unexplained or improperly accumulated wealth.)

“Pati po kung ano ‘yung mekanismo para ma-determine na ‘yun at saka po kung ano ‘yung standards at ano po rin ‘yung mga gawain ng isang usual na government official sa pagtatago ng kanyang mga wealth kasi dahil siya ay very experienced on the matter being Sandiganbayan Justice for a very long time,” he added.

(She would also explain the mechanisms for making that determination, the applicable standards, and the methods government officials might use to conceal their wealth—drawing on her extensive experience, having served as a Sandiganbayan Justice for a very long time.)
The Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment specifically alleges that the Vice President accumulated unexplained wealth through the following:

failure to fully and truthfully disclose all her and her spouse's assets, liabilities, and net worth in her statement of assets, liabilities, and net worth (SALN) including in her SALN for the years 2022, 2023, and 2024; and
failure to divest, and instead, willfully continued, all her business interests during her tenure as vice president for the years 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025.
Tongol said only one person might be presented on Monday as the court expects that the prosecution will exhaust the time available for the testimony of Cabotaje-Tang.

“Knowing the weight of the witness, ayaw naman syempre ng House prosecution panel na sayangin ‘yung appearance ni Justice Tang. And importante rin siguro ‘yung mga sasabihin niya. So magandang, I think the prosecution will make a very good presentation on Monday,” he said.

(Knowing the weight of the witness, the House prosecution panel naturally wouldn’t want to waste Justice Tang’s appearance in court. Her testimony is likely important, too. So, I think the prosecution will make a very good presentation on Monday.)
Should Cabotaje-Tang be qualified as an expert witness, Tongol said that she will still be subject to the cross-examination of the defense team.
“‘Yung opposing counsel magtatanong po ng mga bagay-bagay na pwedeng butasin. ‘Yung one ---‘yung credibility ng expertise niya, kung talagang expert pa siya o hindi,” he explained.
(The opposing counsel will ask questions to try to poke holes in her testimony. One way is by questioning the credibility of her expertise — whether or not she truly qualifies as an expert witness.)
“Pangalawa, ‘yung kanyang conclusions. Paano siya naka-come up ng conclusion? May basehan ba ‘yan sa logic? ‘Yung kanyang conclusions ba ay base do’n sa mga pinakitang mga facts o dokumento?”
(Secondly, is by questioning her conclusions. How did she arrive at them? Is there a logical basis? Are her conclusions grounded in the facts or documents presented?) — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Germany's Zverev wins US Open in golden year
articles.summary: Alexander Zverev has won the US Open for the first time, defeating Ben Shelton in the final. It is Zverev's second Grand Slam win of 2026 after a long wait for his first title, but controversy still…

image.caption: After waiting for years to win his first major title, Zverev has now won 2 this yearImage: Mike Segar/REUTERS

blocks.text: Alexander Zverev has won his second Grand Slam singles title after the German top seed beat Ben Shelton in the final of the US Open on Sunday.
Zverev beat the American, who was making his first appearance in a major final, 6-3, 7-6 (7-2), 5-7, 6-2.

This success caps the best season of Zverev's career. Not only has he now won two of the four Grand Slams in the same season, but he has become just the ninth man to reach at least the semifinals at all four majors in the same season.

"We went 30 years without winning a Grand Slam title and now we've won two in three months," Zverev said on court after his second major win of the year, following his victory at the French Open in June.
"God has seen how hard we've worked and how much we've suffered. 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before," he said as he thanked his coaching team and family.
Great expectations from the start

As a former junior world No. 1, there were great expectations on Zverev from the moment he started his pro career in 2013 at just 16 years old. Titles soon followed, as did a shock early win over Roger Federer in a tournament in his native Germany in 2016.

blocks.caption: Zverev is starting to deliver on the promise he has shown throughout his careerImage: Mike Segar/REUTERS

blocks.text: But the presence of Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic meant Zverev struggled to make a mark in the Grand Slams. After a string of disappointing exits, he had something of a breakthrough in 2020, reaching the semifinals of the Australian Open and the final of the US Open.

With age starting to catch up with at least two of the big three in modern men's tennis, Zverev looked well primed to become a dominant force in the majors. His 2021 Olympic gold felt like it might be just the start.
French Open ends long grand slam wait

But he was unable to make the opportunity count, and the emergence of Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz has made the task even tougher. Finally, this year, Zverev got his hands on a major title, winning at Roland Garros in June. In doing so, he became the first German man to win a singles Grand Slam since Boris Becker in 1996 in the process.

"It was just relief, joy, everything together," he told ATPTour.com. "I didn't realize that I had won the match until I saw my box all jumping around and celebrating. In your mind, you think, 'Well I've got to continue playing', but then I saw my dad raise his arms in the air. That's when it kind of hit me, 'Okay, we've done it. We've achieved it. We are Grand Slam champions'."

Becker's triumph was a year before Zverev was born in Hamburg to Russian parents who were both tennis pros in the Soviet Union and moved to Germany in 1991. His older brother, Mischa, was also a pro until 2023, reaching the quarterfinals of the Australian Open in 2017 and becoming world number 25 in the same year. But it was Alexander who was destined for the even bigger stage.
Family a big influence on Zverev's career

In their youth, Mischa was generally coached by his father, Alexander Zverev Snr, while the younger brother was coached by his mother, Irina. His father has taken the reins in the professional arena though, and the family remain a constant fixture at Zverev's matches.

"I know there are crazy tennis parents out there as well," the 29-year-old said on the subject ahead of the US Open. "If you try to control every single aspect of your kid's life, even when the kid is 25, 26, 27 years old and at some point has a personal life… I think that is never helpful."

"But if you have smart tennis parents like we do have on tour now, I feel like Ben Shelton's father is incredibly smart, Casper Ruud's father is incredibly smart, I feel like I'm lucky enough to say the same thing about my parents. I think then it's beneficial."

blocks.caption: Zverev's triumph in the French Open this year was his first grand slam winImage: Emma Da Silva/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Despite finally ending Germany's long wait for a major male tennis champion, Zverev is far from universally liked in his own country, or on the tennis circuit.
Domestic violence allegations

While there is acknowledgement of his work in promoting awareness of type 1 diabetes, with which he was diagnosed in 2022, allegations of domestic abuse have hung over his career and seen him heckled at various tournaments. His behavior on court has also seen him get in trouble before.

The first came in October 2020, when his ex-girlfriend, Olya Sharypova, claimed he had been violent towards her on multiple occasions. However, Sharypova didn't press criminal charges, and in January 2023, men's tennis governing body the ATP closed its own investigation into the matter, citing "insufficient evidence."
Welcoming that decision at the time, Zverev said: "From the beginning, I have maintained my innocence and denied the baseless allegations made against me."

But he faced a Berlin court in 2024 after similar allegations from Brenda Patea, Zverev's ex-girlfriend and the mother of his daughter. The court was told that "after a heated argument" in the German capital, Zverev allegedly pushed Patea against a wall and strangled her with both hands.

He denied the charges and the case was settled, with Zverev paying €200,000 ($233,000), €150,000 of which went to the state and €50,000 to charitable organizations. The case was officially declared "no verdict" and Zverev made no admission of guilt.

articles.title: Historic first BARMM parliamentary polls kick off; over 5,000 precincts open
articles.summary: The first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) kicked off on Monday, September 14, 2026, as over 5,000 voting precincts opened across the region.

blocks.text: Published September 14, 2026 6:00am
The first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) kicked off on Monday, September 14, 2026, as over 5,000 voting precincts opened across the region.
In the course of election day, priority voters — including senior citizens, persons with disabilities (PWDs), and pregnant women—can take advantage of early voting hours from 5:00 a.m. to 7:00 a.m.
Meanwhile, regular voting hours will run from 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.

Priority voters may still cast their ballots during regular voting hours and will retain priority queue access. All designated priority polling areas are located on the ground floor of voting centers.

Voters are expected to select one regional parliamentary political party, one district representative, and six sectoral representatives (two for Settler Communities, and one each for Women, Youth, Ulama, and Traditional Leaders).
Voters are allowed to bring a prepared list or sample ballot ("kodigo") of their chosen candidates, provided it reflects their personal selections.
The election is expected to yield 80 parliamentary members composed of 40 Regional Parliamentary Party Representatives, 32 parliamentary district representatives, and 8 sectoral representatives.
The Commission on Elections (Comelec) previously stated that it targets a full proclamation within two days.
To ensure peace and order throughout the elections, the Philippine National Police (PNP) has been on full alert in BARMM since September 11.
Comelec Chairman George Garcia urged the public to report any anomalies that may hamper the peaceful and organized conduct of the elections.

A total of 108 observers representing 16 international organizations are also monitoring the historic polls, according to the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity (OPAPRU).

They are scheduled to oversee election activities in Cotabato City, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, the Special Geographic Area, Marawi City, Lamitan, Isabela, Bongao, and Zamboanga City. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: 'I never felt the pressure': Guerrero Jr. finally hits first homer of season at Rogers Centre in win over Os
articles.summary: For the first time this season, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has homered north of the border. The 2023 Home Run Derby champion, Guerrero connected off Baltimore's Trevor Rogers in the fifth inning of…

image.caption: Toronto Blue Jays first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. hits a solo home run during the fifth inning of the team's 8-1 victory over the Baltimore Orioles at Rogers Centre on Sunday. (Vaughn Ridley/Getty Images)

blocks.text: MLB

For the first time this season, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has homered north of the border. The 2023 Home Run Derby champion, Guerrero connected off Baltimore's Trevor Rogers in the fifth inning of Sunday's 8-1 win.
'Vlad's our guy. It's just nice to get that out of the way,' says manager Schneider after 8-1 win
Vladimir Guerrero Jr. claimed he never felt pressure, or thought it was time, to finally smack his first homer at home this season as he made his way to Rogers Centre in recent weeks.

The Toronto Blue Jays' slumping slugger did just that on Sunday, drilling a homer down the left-field line and into his club's bullpen in Toronto's 8-1 drubbing of the Baltimore Orioles (72-78). Bullpen catcher Matt Domian made a nifty catch as part of the moment.
"I knew it was going to happen," Guerrero said through an interpreter. "Today, tomorrow, I never felt the pressure. I never came to the ballpark thinking I had to hit one."
Guerrero enjoyed a four-hit game with two singles and a third-inning double that missed being a homer by a foot off the right-centre field wall.

The homer was the middle of three successive longballs for the home side off Baltimore lefty Trevor Rogers (10-10). First, George Springer knocked a shot out to right field. Then came Guerrero's long-awaited blast. Finally, Kazuma Okamoto followed with a monster 410-footer to the second deck in left.
SAY IT WITH US: #PLAKATA 💥 pic.twitter.com/wFT6GkwVnG—BlueJays

It was the seventh time in club history the Blue Jays slammed three successive homers and the first time since June 19, 2012, when Colby Rasmus, Jose Bautista and Edwin Encarnacion went deep in Milwaukee. It was another seven years before Vernon Wells, Corey Koskie and Shea Hillenbrand went back-to-back at Rogers Centre on April 9, 2005.

Not only did the 41,805 at Rogers Centre go bonkers with Guerrero's homer, but so did his teammates. Shortstop Andres Gimenez and others flew over the top dugout railing in a frenzy to congratulate their teammate.
"It means a lot," Guerrero said. "They obviously were aware of what was going on. They kept telling me to keep my head up."

He sure took his time trotting around the bases. Maybe he was trying to remember his homer routine, like the hop he does between second and third, the shush sign with third-base coach Carlos Febles, the kiss of the wrists and glance skyward as he approaches home plate.
"That's just my pace," he claimed.

items: Urgency level high as Blue Jays look to make push for playoff spot

blocks.text: As Guerrero slipped on the Blue Jays homer blazer for the first time at Rogers Centre since Game 6 against the Seattle Mariners in the 2025 American League Championship Series on Oct. 19, the capacity crowd chanted "Vla-ddy, Vla-ddy," for a curtain call that Guerrero obliged.
"I think everyone was pretty excited, not just for him, but for the game, too." Toronto manager John Schneider added. "It seemed like the crowd really sensed what it actually meant to."
The reaction was far from the boos he occasionally heard at home.
"My father [former Montreal Expos standout Vladimir Guerrero Sr.] always told me that the fans don't boo bad players," Guerrero said when asked about the jeers.

The 27-year-old Guerrero hit his homer in his 68th home game of 2026 and 252nd at-bat. But he wasn't the only offensive highlight for the Blue Jays (75-75), who remain one game behind the Cleveland Guardians for the final AL wild-card spot.
Springer knocked in four RBI with his rally-igniting homer and a bases-loaded clearing double in the eighth. Okamoto's homer meant he set a rookie club record with his 85th RBI.
"It was great, a game like that," Guerrero said. "But it's about winning, it's about the team."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Tim has covered the hockey landscape and other sports in Canada for three decades for The Canadian Press, CBC Sports, the Globe and Mail and Toronto Sun. He has been to three Winter Olympics, 11 Stanley Cups, a world championship as well as 17 world junior championships, 13 Memorial Cups and 13 University Cups. The native of Waterloo, Ont., always has his eye out for an underdog story.

articles.title: ‘Sweat the asset’: new development minister plots path to make UK aid count
articles.summary:
Kirsty McNeill reaffirms Labour’s 0.7% of GDP pledge and promises value for money to allay voter concerns

The development minister, Kirsty McNeill, has declared herself “a huge believer in…

blocks.text: The development minister, Kirsty McNeill, has declared herself “a huge believer in aid”, as she reaffirmed Labour’s manifesto pledge to return to a target of 0.7% of national income spending.

McNeill, a former adviser to Gordon Brown and senior executive at Save the Children, declined to give any timetable, repeating the formula that the government would work towards the target “when fiscal circumstances allow”.
But she made a full-throated argument for the benefits of aid – as well as promising to build new “agile partnerships” to work on development challenges.

“I’m a huge believer in aid; I’m a huge believer in the quality of British aid, and when you have more of it, you can have more impact. And I think it’s important that colleagues hear that underscored,” she said.

Repeating the manifesto pledge that Labour made before the 2024 general election to return to 0.7% – instead slashing aid the next year – McNeill insisted that in the Burnham government, “everyone from the prime minister down is a believer in the spirit that animated that manifesto”.
McNeill will be setting out her priorities in a speech to charities and campaigners at the New Economics Foundation thinktank on Monday.
She will announce that the government is making up to £15m available via its humanitarian crisis fund to support preventive action in countries most at risk from El Niño.

“It will just do very practical things like vaccinate livestock and get cash to farmers to provide supplies,” she said. The UN has warned that the climate phenomenon is likely to be the most severe in 1,000 years, exacerbating risks of wildfires and flooding.

The 0.7% aid target was adopted by the Blair government and became a cross-party consensus, until it was set aside by Rishi Sunak in the depths of the Covid pandemic, as the government rapidly stepped up domestic spending.

Charities have warned that Labour’s more recent aid cuts, taking spending to 0.3% of national income, are causing sharp reductions in bilateral UK support to some of the world’s poorest countries. McNeill’s predecessor, Jenny Chapman, took the job after Anneliese Dodds quit over the scale of the cuts.

At the time of Starmer’s decision, some Labour strategists were concerned about what they perceived as the unpopularity of aid spending among voters. But McNeill said Labour should not be afraid to make a straightforward argument for development.

blocks.caption: McNeill, a former adviser to Gordon Brown, has served as the minister of state for international development since July. Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian

blocks.text: “As we’ve lost our confidence, we started trying to make lots of different arguments for development that go beyond what I believe to be the core one, which is, if you have the capability to save people’s lives and to change people’s lives, you should deploy that capability ambitiously,” she said.

“I think aid is a really good instrument to save children’s lives. And the impacts of British aid, through immunisation, or by feeding children who would otherwise starve, is one that in every conversation with the public I’ve had, whether it’s with a constituent on the doorstep or in my previous job at Save the Children, when you’re saying, ‘Do you think if we can do that, we should do that?’ people say: ‘Yes, we should.’”

Voters’ concerns are more about the value for money and effectiveness of aid spending, she said, promising to “sweat the asset” when it came to getting the best out of the current straitened resources.

She said she saw her role as bringing all the expertise and leverage of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) to bear on what she called the “five securities” – “health security, climate security, food security, human security and economic security”.
“The focus on securities is an attempt to recast my job as being about global cooperation and how we get security through solidarity,” she added.
“That will mean pressing for reform of some of the international bodies that spend UK aid, as well as forming ‘bespoke partnerships’, to work on specific issues.”

A veteran of the Make Poverty History campaign in the mid-2000s, McNeill contrasted this approach with that of the Blair government, which used the UK chairing of the G8 group of industrialised countries in 2005 to secure significant debt relief for developing countries.

“Many of us came of age at a time when there were summits with big announcements, and a cheque from the UK government, and actually the thing that I want to be held to account for is have I done the grind, the diplomatic grind, to get the maximum we can out of our relationships?”
McNeill has been the MP for Midlothian, south of Edinburgh, since 2024, winning the constituency from the Scottish National party.

Her boss, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has signalled that he wants development to be a more prominent focus of the FCDO’s work, including by directly taking up the UK’s seat on the World Bank board.

“The foreign secretary’s been very clear that both development and climate are going to be at the heart of British policy: they’re not an addition, they’re right at the beating heart, which I’m obviously absolutely delighted about,” she said.

articles.title: Andy Burnham to host entrepreneurs and local mayors at No 10 on Monday
articles.summary:
Prime minister vows to ‘reindustrialise Britain’ through new partnership with business

The prime minister is to host business leaders, entrepreneurs and local mayors at Downing Street on…

blocks.text: The prime minister is to host business leaders, entrepreneurs and local mayors at Downing Street on Monday to pitch his government as a “partner for growth” that can offer a stable platform for investment and jobs in the UK.

Ahead of the event, Andy Burnham said the country had “everything it needs to succeed”, including talented people and world-class universities, but requires “a culture shift in how Britain does business” if it is to unlock its full potential.

The new prime minister vowed to “reindustrialise Britain” through a new partnership with business. “That means putting government firmly on the side of the people who take risks, start companies, create jobs and bring new ideas to life,” he said.

“It means ensuring ambition is rewarded, making it easier to start and grow a business and giving people the confidence that if they have a great idea, they’ll get all the support they need to bring it to life.”

Burnham will host a roundtable with entrepreneurs – including the founders of Octopus Energy, Revolut and Starling Bank and quantum computing companies including Oxford Quantum Circuits – before welcoming chief executives from some of Britain’s largest businesses for a reception in No 10 along with regional mayors.

They include the bosses of financial companies HSBC, Aviva and Standard Chartered, supermarkets Morrisons and Sainsbury’s, telecoms groups BT and Vodafone, oil companies BP and Shell and manufacturers Rolls-Royce and BAE Systems.
Monday’s round of meetings come as Burnham and John Healey, the chancellor, prepare for their first budget on 28 October.

Burnham has vowed to deliver growth across the country and to devolve power and resources away from Westminster to do so. But Healey faces a tough task, presenting his budget amid rising borrowing costs and the impact of the Iran war on the global economy.
Although the economy unexpectedly grew by 0.4% in July, boosted by AI and cloud computing, economists have warned rising energy costs may have held back growth in August and September.

Suren Thiru, chief economist for the Institute of Chartered Accountants England and Wales, said the chancellor could be left with a “budget headache” if economic growth starts to dwindle, as more muted growth and surging borrowing costs erode his fiscal headroom, raising the prospect of further tax rises.

Both Burnham and Healey have stressed their commitment to the fiscal rules laid down by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, which require day-to-day spending to be covered by taxes and government debt to fall as a share of the economy by 2029/30. They are also bound by Labour’s manifesto commitment not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT.

In his first major speech as chancellor last week, Healey said boosting economic growth would be his defining mission as chancellor but also warned Labour had to “be honest” about the need to control public spending at next month’s budget.
He talked of putting more power and resources into the hands of local leaders, reducing the cost of doing business and using public investment to attract private capital.

articles.title: Politics live: electrifying push for Australians to save $5,000 a year; bumper weekend for auctions
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live

  • Get our new political email, free app…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 12m agoOne Nation reveals ‘net-negative’ migration policy
38m agoBumper weekend for auctions
38m agoLabor announces $300m grants for crisis accommodation
38m agoSave $5,000 by electrifying, organisations say

blocks.text: Health minister says One Nation plan would devastate critical industries
The health minister, Mark Butler, says Pauline Hanson’s plan to cut temporary visas by 750,000 over three years would kill critical industries.
Speaking to reporters in the press gallery corridor this morning, Butler says it would cause serious economic damage – particularly to construction and aged care sectors.

double quotation markPauline Hanson said a few weeks ago, she didn’t care what the impact of her migration policy would be on business, but this is just another level entirely. This is going to smash industries like construction. It would devastate the health sector and aged care and disability.

The government has stalled on its own migration plan that was initially supposed to be announced by home affairs minister, Tony Burke more than a month ago. Butler remains tight lipped over when Burke will make the announcement.
One Nation reveals ‘net-negative’ migration policy
One Nation is targeting international students and the families of skilled migrants in its proposal to cut 750,000 temporary visa holders in Australia over three years.
The move would return temporary visa numbers back to 2017 levels.

Hanson says net migration under the plan would be “net-negative” for the first three years, and then sit at 130,000 – however who knows what that actually means because when One Nation recently announced this, none of its MPs seemed to be able to define what net migration was.

For those playing at home, net migration measures people coming into or leaving the country for a period of at least 12 months over 16 months and thus excludes tourists. Much of the confusion was around whether backpackers and people on the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme would count under the Nom.
About 10% of the temporary visas to be cut would include people living in Australia who don’t have a visa and have exhausted all options to stay.

blocks.caption: Krishani Dhanji

blocks.text: Krishani Dhanji
Good morning, Krishani Dhanji here with you for another busy sitting week.

There’s a few moving parts in Parliament this week – One Nation has this morning announced a migration plan that will drastically cut temporary visas, and lead to more headache for the Coalition who are asked why Pauline Hanson is driving the agenda and not them.
Speaking of Hanson, her fight with Andrew Hastie shows no sign of ending – we’ll likely hear more back and forth from the pair today.

And, the government could look to water down its digital duty of care laws after hints from the communications minister Anika Wells yesterday that she was willing to negotiate on the ministerial powers in the bill.
Let’s get stuck in!
Save $5,000 by electrifying, organisations say

Australian households could save $5,000 a year by electrifying their homes and cars, AAP reports, and more than 30 organisations will call for incentives and stronger policies in Canberra as part of a national campaign.
The campaign is linked to the international Electrify Now campaign, and follows a COP31 push to raise the global electrification rate from about 20% to 35% by 2035.

Groups including Energy Consumers Australia, the Electric Vehicle Council, Farmers for Climate Action, and Rewiring Australia will launch the campaign at Parliament House, calling for changes to help more Australians replace equipment powered by gas, petrol or diesel.
Energy Efficiency Council policy head Jeremy Sung said:

double quotation markThere’s a role for the Australian government to send a clear signal that electrification is happening and that it’s what the future of our energy system will depend on. At the moment, federal policy is sending mixed messages.
Labor announces $300m grants for crisis accommodation
The government is giving $300m in grants to build crisis and transitional accomodation, that will deliver 500 new homes and support around 19,000 vulnerable Australians.

The housing minister, Clare O’Neil and social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, say the total crisis housing package will support more than 50,000 women and children escaping family violence, and help young people at risk of or already experiencing homelessness.
But the money itself isn’t new: it was previously announced as concessional loans for the sector to help build the accommodation, and will now instead provide direct grants following consultations.
The grants will go to providers including state governments, community housing providers and First Nations organisations.
Plibersek said in a statement:

double quotation markToo often we ask, “why didn’t she leave?,” when we should have asked, where would she go? We know that safe housing is absolutely critical to help women and children leave violence. That’s why we are building more than ever before.
Bumper weekend for auctions

blocks.caption: Cait Kelly

blocks.text: Cait Kelly
Data from Cotality has shown auction rates were up over the weekend, with almost 60% of homes selling – the highest peak in 19 weeks.
The national preliminary clearance rate hit 58.5%, a small jump from the 52.7% recorded last week.
Experts have warned that Australia’s penchant for auctions – we are among the few countries that regularly use them – has helped push prices up.
While the weekend rate was up, there is still an overall decline in the number of houses being sold through auctions.
Speaking to the Australian Financial Review on Sunday, Cotality’s Tim Lawless said the rise in clearance rates should be viewed against a longer-term plunge in volumes.
double quotation markThe number of auctions held was up 11.4% on a week ago – but held more than 30 per cent lower than a year ago.
Welcome to Guardian Australia’s live coverage for Monday.
Krishani Dhanji will be joining us shortly.
Let’s begin.

articles.title: Swedish party blocs tied after Sunday vote, projections say
articles.summary: With 50% of the votes counted, the two main blocs were separated by only 20,000 votes, Sweden public broadvasteer SVT said.

blocks.text: Sweden has two major political blocs featuring four parties on the right and four on the left - meaning coalition and minority governments are relatively common.
Andersson's party, the Social Democrats, have been a major force in Swedish politics since the end of World War Two.
But SD - founded by Nazi sympathisers in the 1980s - had been shunned for years until 2022 when it became the country's second largest party after campaigning on violent crime and immigration.

After casting her vote on Sunday, Andersson laid out the choice facing the Swedish public: "Should we have a government entirely dominated by the Sweden Democrats, something that has never happened in Sweden before? Or should we have a government led by me, which will steer Sweden in a new spirit of co-operation?"
Kristersson, for his part, said it was important he and his alliance were able to continue their work.
"I think there is a genuine enthusiasm for us being able to continue our important work," he said after casting his ballot in his home municipality of Strangnas.
National security, gang crime and welfare spending dominated the election campaign.

articles.title: Departin' from Parton: Nashville International Airport to be renamed in Dolly Parton's honour
articles.summary: It's official. The late Dolly Parton will be gaining a new namesake — and it's taking off. Nashville International Airport in Tennessee is set to be renamed in honour of the celebrated singer, after…

image.caption: Dolly Parton is shown during Dolly: An Original Musical fireside chat and news conference at the Fisher Center for the Performing Arts in Nashville on Jan. 28, 2025. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

It's official. The late Dolly Parton will be gaining a new namesake — and it's taking off. Nashville International Airport in Tennessee is set to be renamed in honour of the celebrated singer, after its board of commissioners voted in favour of the move on Friday.
The airport's board of commissioners voted in favour of the move on Friday
It's official. The late Dolly Parton will be gaining a new namesake — and it's taking off.
Nashville International Airport in Tennessee is set to be renamed in honour of the celebrated singer, after its board of commissioners voted in favour of the move on Friday.

The idea was first floated last year but gained momentum following Parton's death last month at the age of 80. A social media campaign by fans to rename the airport in honour of the queen of country picked up steam, particularly after Nashville Mayor Freddie O'Connell and Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee threw their support behind the proposal late last month.

items: Tennessee intends to rename Nashville airport after Dolly Parton, governor says

blocks.text: "Dolly Parton's extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state," Lee said in a statement at the time.

"At a place where Tennessee welcomes the world, it is fitting that Nashville International Airport would bear the name of our state's favourite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly's music, generosity, faith, and kindness."

Following Friday's decision, Lee said in a statement posted to his X account that it "was an important step to honour her remarkable legacy" as "Dolly has always helped the world fall in love with Tennessee."
He could have been referring to the estimated $1.8 billion and counting that the singer brings into the state each year through her Dollywood theme park.

items: Dolly Parton, one of country music's greatest legends, dead at 80

blocks.text: Or, perhaps, to the fact that she was born in Tennessee — coming into the world on Jan. 19, 1946, in Pittman Center, and growing up in a one-room cabin in nearby Locust Ridge.

The legendary singer would go on to put Tennessee in the global spotlight, appearing at the Grand Ole Opry, Nashville's weekly country music concert at just 13 years old. After high school, she moved to Nashville to pursue a career in music.

There's no word yet on how long the renaming process is expected to take, though the airport's current policy prohibits naming any property after a person who has not been dead for at least two years, the New York Times reported.
Dolly Parton's trailblazing influence and songwriting legacy

The exact name of the airport in Parton's honour has also yet to be selected. However, the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority said in a statement that it was "working closely with the appropriate parties to thoughtfully determine how Dolly Parton's name and legacy will be incorporated."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kayla McLean is a web journalist with CBC News in Toronto. She grew up in Brampton, Ont., and received her bachelor of arts in media production at Toronto Metropolitan University. Before joining CBC in 2024, she worked as a breaking news reporter at Global News Toronto — covering everything from crime, sports, festivals and politics. She also reported for Global News's current affairs show, The New Reality, covering stories with a focus on racial equality and climate justice. She also previously held positions as a chase producer and writer for CTV News Channel.
