articles.title: New Charlie Kirk statue vandalized at Turning Point USA headquarters
articles.summary:
The 8ft statue, installed in Phoenix last week to mark one year since Kirk’s killing, was found painted red

A newly unveiled statue of the rightwing activist Charlie Kirk was vandalized at…

blocks.text: A newly unveiled statue of the rightwing activist Charlie Kirk was vandalized at the Turning Point USA headquarters in Phoenix, Arizona.
The statue was found with red spray-paint. A nearby poster memorial in front of the statue was vandalized with red paint as well.

“We will restore the statue and replace the signs, but we are also reviewing the footage of the incident and are working with law enforcement to identify who did this and hold them accountable,” Turning Point USA said in a statement.
The 8ft statue was installed on 10 September to mark the one-year anniversary of Kirk’s killing.
Kirk, a key Donald Trump ally, was shot and killed at a Turning Point USA event in Utah.
A Utah judge recently ruled that the man accused of fatally shooting Kirk must stand trial for aggravated murder, a felony charge that makes him eligible for the death penalty if convicted.

articles.title: San Jose officer fired for misusing Flock camera database in domestic abuse case
articles.summary:
Police officer shared location of a woman with his relative who is accused of abusing woman

A San Jose police officer was fired for using his department’s Flock license plate tracking system…

blocks.text: A San Jose police officer was fired for using his department’s Flock license plate tracking system to share the location of a woman with the suspect accused of abusing her, Chief Paul Joseph told NBC Bay Area on Friday.
The firing marks another in a growing number of cases of misuse of a controversial surveillance technology that has expanded rapidly over the last several years.

The officer accessed Flock camera data last year without authorization on his personal phone for the vehicle of a woman allegedly abused by one of the officer’s family members, then sent that information to his cousin, according to Joseph. The suspect in the domestic abuse case was the officer’s cousin, according to the San Jose Mercury News.
Police discovered the unauthorized access when the woman told police that her alleged abuser told her that he knew her location.
The department immediately placed the officer on administrative leave and began a criminal investigation into his actions, Joseph said.
“I was furious that an officer would betray the public’s trust in that manner, that he would not understand how serious of a violation that is,” Joseph said.

Joseph did not publicly disclose the name of the officer. San Jose police department referred the case to the Santa Clara county district attorney’s office, but the officer was not been charged with a crime. The district attorney’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Joseph told the Mercury News that state lawmakers should pass legislation making it easier to charge such violations as crimes. San Jose police department referred the officer to the commission on peace officer standards and training, which has the power to bar him from working as a law enforcement officer again in the state, the paper reported.

License plate reading technology has drawn broad criticism, recurring protests and vandalism from the right and left alike, as law enforcement has deployed tens of thousands of cameras across the country, raising concerns about privacy, mass surveillance, false positives and police misuse of the technology.

The technology has also raised concerns among immigrant rights groups, as law enforcement agencies increasingly share that data with Immigration and Customs Enforcement that ICE uses to press forward with Trump’s broadly unpopular mass deportation agenda.
Dozens of law enforcement officers have used license-plate readers to stalk women, according to the Institute for Justice, a public interest law firm.
The California assembly adjourned this month without taking action on a bill that would have imposed new regulations on license-plate reading technology.

It marked the fifth straight year that California lawmakers declined to impose new safeguards on license-plate readers like Flock, according to CalMatters. The California assembly passed a bill that would have imposed new regulations, including a mandate to delete data unrelated to an investigation after two months, but Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed it.

articles.title: US schools and police warn about viral ‘Cat in the Hat’ trend after teens’ arrests
articles.summary:
Disturbing and AI-generated versions of Dr Seuss character have been used to threaten schools and communities

Schools and law enforcement authorities in the US are issuing

blocks.text: Schools and law enforcement authorities in the US are issuing warnings against a viral “Cat in the Hat” social media trend in which disturbing or AI-generated versions of the Dr Seuss character are used to threaten students, schools and communities.
The latest warnings come as safety concerns increase and several teenagers have been arrested or charged over posts connected to the trend.

The Cat in the Hat trend originated on Snapchat as images or short videos showing a disturbing version of the Cat in the Hat, often resembling the character played by Mike Myers in the 2003 live-action film, lurking outside homes, schools or on streets at night.

Some footage appears to be AI-generated, while other posts include real people wearing costumes. Additionally, some videos include threatening messages towards specific towns or schools. More disturbing versions named individuals or included lists of supposed targets.
The posts originally circulated in Ireland and the United Kingdom in August 2026 before quickly becoming viral in parts of the United States and Canada, the BBC reported.
Even though social media users view the trend as a hoax or prank, authorities are warning that causing people to fear for their safety could potentially constitute as criminal harassment.
Recently, near Wichita, Kansas, a 15-year-old was arrested after allegedly posting a video on social media that made ominous threats toward students using the trend.

A statement shared by the Hutchinson police department said that during the investigation, officers determined that a 15-year-old Hutchinson high school student created a TikTok account for that community referencing the Cat in the Hat trend. The juvenile was ultimately charged with two counts of criminal threat.

“Threats of any nature are taken seriously by the Hutchinson Police Department and Hutchinson High School. Regardless of whether a post is intended as a joke, it is unlawful to cause others, particularly students, to fear for their safety,” the statement added.
Similarly, in Worth county, Georgia, two students at Worth county high school are facing charges after the school district said they participated in the viral social media hoax.
Both students involved are being charged, and will also face disciplinary action, school officials say.
Due to the potential threats caused by the trend, some school communities have also increased their police presence as a precautionary measure.

In a statement released by the Grand Junction police department in Colorado, it said that it increased its presence at West middle school and Grand Junction high school “out of an abundance of caution” after the circulation of a Cat in the Hat post. The post led to the arrest of a 14-year old student.

As the trend continues to circulate, law enforcement authorities are urging students to report any safety concerns to a trusted adult, school administrator or law enforcement official rather than reposting or sharing the content.

articles.title: JD Vance’s Catholicism could be at odds with Maga evangelicals in 2028
articles.summary:
Vice-president wears religion on his sleeve but winding spiritual path could alienate evangelicals and Catholics

US vice-president JD Vance has worn his religion on his sleeve since…

blocks.text: US vice-president JD Vance has worn his religion on his sleeve since converting to the Catholicism in 2019. He recently published a book, Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith, and memorably met the late Pope Francis at the Vatican on Easter Sunday in 2025, a day before the pontiff died.

But his religious identity could take on new weight as he positions himself for a presidential run in 2028, in which a successful campaign would make him only the third Catholic president in US history. Vance’s winding spiritual path – combined with his avowed evangelical roots – have the potential to stymie him, as he seeks to retain the Christian nationalist voters that have sustained Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement while wooing fellow Catholics.

His presidential ambitions and religious convictions were both on show in a keynote speech to the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday evening, where he invoked scripture and the Apostle Paul in paying homage to the rightwing activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated last year.
“We live in the city of man, not the city of God,” Vance said. “But I believe that our founders built this nation on a promise that echoes our creator.”
The address amounted to “the beginning of 2028 Republican primary competition”, according to Larry Jacobs, a political scientist at the University of Minnesota.

“Vance has thrown his hat in the ring,” he said. “One of the dimensions that JD Vance is bringing to the Republican ticket is the white Christian nationalism. He is trying to put together a coalition that will support him, and he wants the white Christian nationalists to be a key part of that.”

One impediment to that, some religious analysts say, is his conversion to Catholicism – something they believe could leave him with an identity crisis that alienates both evangelicals and Catholic voters.
Both ways

Vance expounded on his beliefs and the evangelical influences that shaped his upbringing in a recent interview with Bryce Crawford, a 22-year-old Christian podcaster with 929,000 subscribers on YouTube.

Commentators say his dilemma was crystallized when Crawford asked for his views on “end times”, an event signifying the second coming of Christ that is much discussed in evangelicalism, but much less so in Catholicism.
Vance expressed a long-held fascination with “end times” beliefs – saying that he had owned a John Hagee bible, which emphasizes end times teachings – before subtly trying to sidestep the issue.

He said: “What I’m trying to focus on is doing as much of God’s work as possible right now, and if that leads to the end times, OK. And if that leads to, you know, us building a better world that thrives and survives for a very long time after I’m gone, that’s great too.

“I just think you’ve got to kind of try to have an attitude of the end times may be coming. In fact, they are coming. It’s just a question of whether they’re coming thousands of years down the road, or a few months down the road, and we’ve got a lot of work to do right now. I‘ve got to try to do the work I can right now.”
The response showed Vance trying to “have things both ways”, suggested Robert Jones, president and founder of the Public Religion Research Institute.

“It reminded me of the kind of conversation that young evangelical men would have sitting around in their dorm room at university,” argued Jones, who comes from an evangelical Christian background. “He’s basically saying, ‘I have no stake in the debate.’
“Anyone schooled inside that evangelical debate would find that position either dismissive of theological of deep theological concerns, or deeply uninformed about them.”

After Pope Leo XIV criticized the Trump administration over the Iran war this year, Vance risked upsetting Catholic voters by telling the pontiff to be “careful” if he was “going to opine on matters of theology”.

The exchange followed an earlier difference of opinion with Pope Francis, in February 2025, when Vance invoked the medieval Christian concept of “ordo amoris” – which translates from Latin as order of love – to justify the Trump administration’s hardline policy of detaining and expelling undocumented people.

“You love your family, and then you love your neighbor, and then you love your community, and then you love your fellow citizens in your own country,” he wrote on social media. “And then after that, you can focus and prioritize the rest of the world.”
The late pope wrote an open letter rejecting the idea and citing the parable of the Good Samaritan.
‘A huge threat’

Daniel Hummel, director of the Lumen Center, a Christian research group in Madison, Wisconsin, said Vance’s public statements highlighted potential pitfalls as he tries to win over both evangelicals and Catholics.
“Vance is a recent Catholic convert, and he still talks a lot like an evangelical,” he said.

That, in itself, could be sufficient to antagonize even conservative Catholics, warned Hummel. “There’s a certain way that Catholics, even conservative Catholics, who might actually disagree with the pope – his view on the Iran war, or something – but respect the pope and would never speak ill of whatever he says, versus an evangelical tradition, where … it’s fine to tell Christian leaders to stay in their lane.”

Vance, who has said he drifted from his evangelical upbringing into atheism by the time he joined the US Marines Corps, may face a further barrier to his political ambitions through a lack of clarity around his religious views.

“It’s pretty clear to me that he understands himself to be a Christian, who is being driven into politics in part because of his Christian faith,” said Hummel. “But it’s unclear to me – even as someone who observes him regularly – what exactly is the content of that Christianity.
“It’s unclear sort of where he’s actually drawing his ideas from when it comes to political theology or how he understands the relationship between religion and politics.

“I think that’s a huge threat to him, because he’s with communities that have strong opinions on these things, and talk about them in very certain ways. So there’s a danger he’ll either commit too much to one side, or the other, and then alienate the other side.”
Authenticity

Jacobs, the University of Minnesota political scientist, said Vance – once a fierce critic of Trump, and warned that he could be “America’s Hitler” – could be derailed by less abstract factors than theological differences.

“The challenge with Vance is authenticity,” he said. “The thing with Trump is the guy resonated authenticity with a variety of Americans, even if the reality behind the scenes would suggest otherwise. He came off as someone who meant what he said.
“But JD Vance too often comes off as someone who is playing the political game.”

Jones said Vance’s appeal to Christian values was underpinned by demographic factors that showed self-identified Republicans to be “more than two-thirds white and Christian”. “A majority of them explicitly support this Christian nationalist movement,” he said.

Vance’s interview with Crawford revealed a further “deeply troubling” trait in his religious beliefs, according to Jones, when the vice-president professed to seeing God’s actions in small coincidences.

The vice-president cited the failed assassination attempt against Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. Shots fired by a lone gunman left Trump with a grazed ear, but killed one rallygoer and critically injured two others.

Vance appeared to attribute that to divine providence, noting that Trump had bowed his head slightly to look at a chart on immigration at the instant the bullet passed. If Trump had been killed, he argued, millions of Americans would not have accepted the election result, and the US would have been irreparably split.

Jones said: “A view like that, un-interrogated – especially from a leader as high up as he is – is quite dangerous, because it is always interpreted as the hand of providence when it is something that favors you.

“If Trump had been killed that day, he even says he would not have taken that as the hand of God. He would have taken that as a grand conspiracy. So that tells you right there that the hand of God will only be seen in things that benefit you.”
The Guardian contacted Vance’s office for comment.

articles.title: Surrey, B.C., man awarded $275K after 77-day-long protest in front of his home
articles.summary: Yun Fei Zhu, the group "leader," was found to have made and published defamatory statements against Bing Chen Gao, a journalist and outspoken critic of the Chinese Communist Party.

image.caption: A screenshot from a YouTube livestream, posted by an account that appears to be linked to Bing Chen Gao, shows protestors holding up signs in a cul-de-sac. (Youtube)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Yun Fei Zhu, the group "leader," was found to have made and published defamatory statements against Bing Chen Gao, a journalist and outspoken critic of the Chinese Communist Party.
Protestors gathered in front of Bing Chen Gao's Surrey house for 77 days straight in 2020
A B.C. journalist has won a defamation lawsuit after a 77-day-long protest in front of his Surrey house in 2020.
In a Thursday decision, B.C. Supreme Court Justice Richard Hewson awarded Bing Chen Gao $275,000, finding defendant Yun Fei Zhu had published defamatory statements about him.
Gao testified that Zhu and others protested outside his home daily, starting Sept. 15, 2020, until Dec. 1, 2020.
Crowds ranged from about 10 to 60 people and the protests were livestreamed, mostly by Zhu, who was treated as a "leader," for about five hours a day to an online audience.
More protests and livestreams took place outside his house in 2023 from Jan. 20 to 25, according to the court document.
Gao said the protesters called him a Chinese Communist Party (CCP) spy, distributed pamphlets disclosing his home address, and played funeral music outside his house.
Guo Wenghui supporters

The protestors were supporters of Chinese tycoon Guo Wenghui, a public critic of the Chinese Communist Party. He started the New Federal State of China (NFSC), a political movement dedicated to replacing the CCP in China.
Two months ago, Guo was sentenced to 30 years in a U.S. prison for fraud.
"Some viewed Guo Wengui as a courageous dissident exposing corruption, while others regarded him and the NFSC as unreliable, conspiratorial and cult‑like," said Hewson’s decision.
It said Gao, who worked as a journalist, was an outspoken critic of Guo.

Gao was also a critic of the CCP — he was involved in the pro-democracy movement in China before he moved to Canada in 2004 — but those who protested outside his house accused him of being "a professional agent long trained by the CCP."
Some of the distributed pamphlets read:

"Gao disguises himself as an anti‑communism activist and has set up a special YouTube channel to spread false information on behalf of the CCP, steer public opinion, and defame real anti-communism activists and the Canadians who are against the CCP."
They also accused Gao of taking money from the CCP.
Throughout the livestreams, protestors could be heard chanting in English and Mandarin "CCP," "stinky dog poop," "trash," "we all hate your guts," and "everybody on this cul-de-sac hates you."
Zhu testified he stopped taking part in the demonstrations after an assault took place in the cul-de-sac, but returned for the protests in 2023.
Gao testified the assault was against a friend of his. He said protests affected his wife, young daughter, and elderly mother-in-law.

items: Blogger vs. businessman: defamation lawsuit rallies supporters in Chinatown

blocks.text: Hewson found Zhu was liable for defamatory comments made by himself and other speakers during the livestreams that he published.
Gao was awarded $250,000 in general damages and a further $25,000 in aggravated damages.
Hewson also ordered an injunction prohibiting Zhu from repeating defamatory statements and ordered him to pay Gao $5,000 in court costs.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Michelle Gomez is a writer and reporter at CBC Vancouver. You can contact her at michelle.gomez@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Prince Harry and Meghan's U.K. return gets a very British roast in Saturday Night Live UK sketch
articles.summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s highly publicized return to England got the full Saturday Night Live UK treatment — and in true British fashion, the welcome was served with a distinctly chilly…

image.caption: Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, arrive to meet volunteer first responders during a visit to Australia's Bondi Beach on April 17. (Jonathan Brady/Pool Photo/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s highly publicized return to England got the full Saturday Night Live UK treatment — and in true British fashion, the welcome was served with a distinctly chilly reception.
The 4-minute bit took aim at Netflix deal, Meghan's lifestyle empire and Royal Family tensions

Prince Harry and his wife Meghan's highly publicized return to England got the full Saturday Night Live UK treatment — and in true British fashion, the welcome was served with a distinctly chilly reception.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex were mocked during the Season 2 premiere of the late-night show on Saturday night.

The four-minute, 52-second bit took aim at, among other things, the couple's deal with Netflix, Meghan's television and business ventures, and the Royal Family's long-running controversies surrounding race.

items: Prince Harry and wife Meghan arrive in U.K.

blocks.text: The cold open began with Harry and Meghan, played by Jack Shep and Ayoade Bamgboye, visiting King Charles and Queen Camilla, portrayed by Larry Dean and Emma Sidi, at a sketch-set version of Balmoral Castle — the Scottish estate where Charles traditionally spends his summer retreat.
"Daddy, I'm home!" Harry proclaims to his father as he walks through the doorway. But the make-believe monarch seems less than pleased to see his son.
"Harry, what are you two doing here?" he scowls. "This castle is for royals only."
The fictional couple reveal that they are moving back to the U.K. "and need your help."
That sets the stage for Charles's withering indictment of the couple's finances and post-royal ventures.

"Don’t tell me you spent all your Netflix money already," Charles bemoans, referring to the multi-year production deal the couple signed with Netflix after they left the U.K. and stepped down as working royals in 2020. According to People, the five-year contract came to an end in 2025 after Netflix chose not to renew the deal under the same terms.
"Daddy, it was $60 million. How long was it meant to last?" Harry responded, drawing laughs from the studio audience.

items: How will the British press cover Harry and Meghan this time around?

blocks.text: Under the Netflix deal, the Sussexes produced several projects, including the wildly popular docuseries Harry & Meghan and Meghan's upbeat lifestyle and cooking program, With Love, Meghan.

Meghan used the latter Netflix series as a promotional platform for her lifestyle brand, As Ever, featuring jams, teas and honeys on the show. That, too, became fodder for Saturday's sketch, which didn't miss the opportunity to poke fun at her attempt to position herself as a lifestyle guru.
"Hey, step-queen, I brought you a gift ... it's ice ... I made it myself," the fictional Meghan told Camilla. "I'm kind of a whiz in the kitchen."
"It's true," Harry added. "She hires the best cooks."

Among the sketch's other biting moments, the writers appeared to reference Harry and Meghan's 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, during which they discussed controversial comments allegedly made within the Royal Family about what colour their son Prince Archie's skin might be.

During Saturday night's cold open, when Camilla greeted the couple, she began by saying, "Hello, sweet Harry," while kissing him on the cheek. Then, turning to the fictional Meghan, she said: "And beautiful Meghan, as brown as ever."

The segment then transitioned into a spoof of Britain's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, after SNL UK breakout star George Fouracres — portraying Burnham — burst into the room. The remainder of the skit focused on teasing Burnham's perceived obsession with being viewed as a "regular guy" while Prince Harry and Meghan ignored him and canoodled in the background.

The Duke and Duchess returned to the U.K. from the United States with their two children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, late last month. The family is expected to live privately outside of London.
No official reason has been given for the relocation. The couple's children have been enrolled in British schools and reportedly started classes this month.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kayla McLean is a web journalist with CBC News in Toronto. She grew up in Brampton, Ont., and received her bachelor of arts in media production at Toronto Metropolitan University. Before joining CBC in 2024, she worked as a breaking news reporter at Global News Toronto — covering everything from crime, sports, festivals and politics. She also reported for Global News's current affairs show, The New Reality, covering stories with a focus on racial equality and climate justice. She also previously held positions as a chase producer and writer for CTV News Channel.

articles.title: Marcos on comments on Martin's arrest: Ask him if it's drama
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has decried critics' statements calling the arrest and subsequent issues, particularly on the health of former Speaker Martin Romualdez, as mere drama.

blocks.text: Published September 14, 2026 2:34am
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has decried critics' statements calling the arrest and subsequent issues, particularly on the health of former Speaker Martin Romualdez, as mere drama.
"See if you talk to him, see if he agrees with you," Marcos told reporters.

Romualdez, a cousin of President Marcos, was arrested on September 7 over plunder charges in connection with flood control projects while he was confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City.
On Friday, Vice President Sara Duterte called the arrest of former Speaker Martin Romualdez "drama" in reaction to a statement of Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla.
Remulla earlier said that her camp wanted her detained and handcuffed for dramatic purposes after a Quezon City court ordered her arrest for grave threats.
Asked for comment about Remulla's remarks, Duterte said it was the Interior Secretary who wanted drama.
“Siya yung may gusto ng drama at saka ang totoong drama kung makikita ninyo ay yung pag-aresto kuno kay Martin Romualdez,” Duterte told reporters.
(He is the one who wants drama, and the real drama, if you notice, is the supposed arrest of Martin Romualdez.)

When asked to comment during a press conference held at the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in India, President Marcos said, "Of course, this is political, right? It is not belief that it is in fact drama."
"It's kind of may masabi e, kailangan may masabi para insultuhin ka or to put you down or sabihin mali iyang ginagawa mo. Basically, pinapatunay niya na wala kang kwentang tao," said Marcos.

"So they have to say that. so that's what they're saying. They are not commenting about... that's not a comment on the procedures of court. It's just another attack. We get them a lot," he added. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Questions mount over what an AI 'slowdown' would look like
articles.summary: While pacing AI development might sound like a quick fix, it is far from an easy solution.

blocks.text: There has been no shortage of warnings from AI's top bosses about existential threats over the years.
I attended the world's first AI safety summit in Bletchley Park in November 2023 where the focus was on the most serious threats imaginable, posed by the most powerful AI models.

At the time, many thought this was in the realm of sci-fi and the real threats were comparatively far more mundane: job losses, cheating in exams. Three years later, many of those same voices don't seem to be so sure.

On Saturday head of AI company Anthropic, Dario Amodei, urged the pace of development to be slowed down - the bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk said they agreed with him.
Meanwhile AI researcher Jacob Coxon - who quit Anthropic - told the BBC on Sunday staff who were developing the systems were "genuinely frightened" for the future of humanity.
They all add up to a chorus of serious voices urging a slowdown, but although it might sound like a quick fix, it is far from an easy solution.
America is widely understood to be terrified of losing the race to build the most powerful AI to China.
On Sunday President Trump made his own views clear, claiming the US was ahead of China in the AI race and declaring: "Whoever wins AI, wins."

China isn't renowned for wanting to come second. Everyone I speak to says that even if their company pauses, others will not and they will just get left behind. It reminds me of the height of the campaign for nuclear disarmament. The problem then too was that nobody wanted to go first.

There is also the question of how on earth a slowdown would be enforced. Who would police it? Would we be relying on the AI companies to be transparent about what they are doing, and more importantly what they are choosing not to do? That would require an epic level of trust, which arguably the tech sector has never earned.

Although Amodei in his post proposed a three-point plan that included independent monitoring of AI models as they are developed, industry-wide regulation and global regulation, some observers question how this would work in practice.
"Nobody has given a substantive explanation of what 'slowdown' means," said Ed Zitron, CEO of EZ Primary Research.
"Putting a plant from METR, where one of the guys who quit Anthropic went, in every AI company? Democratic and global 'co-ordination'? Doesn't mean anything to me."
Zitron said stopping training AI models would leave them vulnerable to Chinese rivals.
"Their margins might improve but their products will be captured in amber and distilled by Chinese labs. They may have to change pricing. I truly don't know how it all works.
"This could burst the bubble. But right now we are very thin on what a 'slowdown' means."

In the UK, we have heard about plans to roll out the tech more widely within the NHS to improve patient care, and how AI gave the UK economy a much-needed boost over the summer. We are all being encouraged to use it more and more at work, in education and in our personal lives.
The industry is a key part of the UK's strategy to drive economic growth. "There is no plan B" a former government adviser told me, so could a slowdown wreck future prospects here in Britain?

The AI industry is burning through enormous amounts of money and natural resources and so far, is not creating nearly as much revenue. There are multiple reports suggesting a number of firms adopting the technology are disappointed by it.

Economists widely speculate that even the current giants are not all likely to survive and that some kind of "levelling" is coming – also known as a bursting bubble. But those firms which do make it could end up becoming the most powerful mega-corporations the world has ever seen, and that comes with its own issues.

OpenAI choosing to halt its march to the stock market could be seen as an epiphany-like moment of taking responsibility for public safety – but it could also be the move of a company which has realised it might not get the lucrative payout it needs while its entire product is perceived to be lethal.

"One of the probably the biggest challenges that we have right now is that no one can predict with certainty how this technology is going to evolve," says Alexander Voicu from the UK AI company Synthesia.

"We know that these systems are getting more powerful, but we don't know where and how they're going to be used, and we haven't figured out essentially a way of taking full advantage of their potential. My only concern in rushing to regulate now, where there's still a lot of open questions, is that it could actually backfire."
We also can't deny the fact that underpinning this entire tech revolution is an ocean of investor cash.
"I'm not worried about the existential risks of AI, I'm worried about the corporate greed of the companies that are creating it," says Sasha Luccioni, the founder of Sustainable AI.
Leading computer scientist Professor dame Wendy Hall, who has advised the UN about AI, says the current crisis is all about the companies not behaving responsibly enough.
She likens the current situation to a farmer having a bull in a field which escapes and causes destruction – and the farmer blames the bull.
"Of course it's not the bull's fault – it's the farmer," she says. Clearly, the fences weren't robust enough, and that is exactly what she says we are seeing with AI guardrails right now.
But if those guardrails become too restrictive, could this spell the end of AI?

Some believe there is a more secretive, politically-motivated push for a rules-based clampdown in order to "regulate AI into oblivion" as Parker Thayer, an investigative researcher at the Conservative-leaning Capital Research Centre think-tank, put it on X this week.
His post was viewed nearly eight million times. It is an extreme and unproven view but it shows that not everybody is on board with the idea of regulation saving the day.
Whatever the reality, the storm currently engulfing the AI industry could already have caused reputational damage to the firms currently in pole position forever.
As Professor Hall puts it: "Would you invest in a company that says it's going to bring about human extinction?"

articles.title: Trade unions, MPs and donors urge Burnham to revisit party funding rules
articles.summary:
PM has so far declined to insert curbs on UK-based donors, despite £72m donations from billionaires to Reform UK

Trade unions, MPs and donors have urged the government to look again at party…

blocks.text: Trade unions, MPs and donors have urged the government to look again at party funding rules, after Reform UK insisted £72m in donations from two crypto billionaires was within the law.
Andy Burnham, a previous backer of caps on domestic donations, has so far declined to insert any curbs in the elections bill that would apply to UK-based donors.

Labour MPs have voiced anger on internal WhatsApp groups that the government did not act last week when the elections bill was in the Commons to restrict domestic donations after two donors – Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo – gave Reform UK a total of £72m over the weekend.
The bill returns to the House of Lords next week where peers told the Guardian they would ask the government to look again at the issue.
The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, suggested on Sunday that the donations could be caught in a new bill which would apply retrospectively on donors from outside the UK.

The two donors who gave Reform £36m each have both previously been based outside the UK. Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong. It is unclear when Delo returned to live in the UK and whether Harborne remains a resident of Thailand. Reform said both donations were within the rules.

Senior government sources indicated the government was prepared to look again at the issue of domestic donations once it receives advice from a newly commissioned taskforce and from the Electoral Commission.

One No 10 source said they did not want to delay the elections bill – which gives votes to 16-year-olds and puts new curbs on foreign donors – but said the bill was “not the right vehicle but this is not the end of the story”.

Several Labour MPs said they had been assured by ministers that further legislation could still come before the general election. Trade unions are also understood to be wavering on the issue and a possible donations cap is expected to be part of discussions at the TUC congress next week, where Rayner and Burnham will speak.

Unions have been central to the decision not to impose a domestic donations cap after several, especially GMB, argued it would be a slippery slope towards future rightwing governments curbing union donations.
On Sunday the Unite trade union said it was in favour of a cap – and the largest trade union, Unison, said it would fight attempts by billionaires to influence politics.
“For individual donors there must be a cap,” said Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary. “I think at some point it gets beyond what people think as normal.”

Andrea Egan, Unison’s general secretary, said: “As his support dwindles in this country, Farage is turning to crypto billionaires in an attempt to undermine our democracy. The trade union movement will oppose him every step of the way.”

Stella Creasy, the Labour MP whose amendment on donations caps attracted support in the Commons, is liaising with peers about how they can raise the issue when the bill returns to the House of Lords this week.

The Labour peer Michael Wills said: “The government has already committed to urgently reviewing the questions of caps on donations. Now the bill is in the Lords, it offers an unmissable opportunity to say when that review will complete its work, and what its remit will be.”

blocks.caption: Stella Creasy’s amendment proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. Photograph: Milo Chandler/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

blocks.text: Creasy said the Reform donations had “concentrated people’s minds about what is now happening in our politics and what it will do to the voices of working people if it’s not stopped – we have the chance with the Lords to amend this bill with a cap”.
Her amendment proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. It was not put to a vote after the government said it would ask a taskforce to look at the proposal.
after newsletter promotion

The former shadow chancellor John McDonnell said it was time for the government to move faster and for unions to get onboard. “It’s clear now to the trade unions meeting in congress this week that action is needed to protect our democracy and there’s a growing expectation the government will respond with urgency,” he said.

Two influential big party donors also called for a cap on Sunday. The billionaire businessman and Phones 4U founder, John Caudwell, who previously donated to the Conservative party in 2019, told BBC Radio 4’s Broadcasting House: “There should be a definite change in law. We should not have very wealthy people making undue influence.”

Dale Vince, the Ecotricity founder who has given donations to the Labour party, said it was “urgent” the government dealt with donations rules. “Ridiculous sums of money don’t level the playing field – they distort it.

“Our current system of funding is anti-democratic – those with big money have more say than the simple vote we all have. A cap on donations would be a step in the right direction – the end game should be publicly funded politics.”

blocks.caption: The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak: ‘We are going to need to restrict the ability of billionaires like Delo to buy and sell our politics.’  Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA

blocks.text: The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, suggested he was sympathetic to further action. Speaking before the opening of the TUC congress, he said: “No one wants the UK to become a country for hire in the way Reform is clearly a party for hire. Without a doubt, we are going to need to restrict the ability of billionaires like Delo to buy and sell our politics. But we’ll have to do that in a way that doesn’t cut across workers having their voice heard politically.”

Reform has said it is confident that its two donors will not be caught in a retrospective cap on donations from Britons living abroad. “We are 100% confident both are legal and won’t ever have to be handed back,” a spokesperson said, suggesting both men would meet the criteria on residency even within the rules of the new bill.

As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March.

Rayner – the minister responsible for the bill – said it was not targeted at individual donors or parties. “We didn’t know that donors were going to be putting that money in, and this isn’t about individual donors to a political party. This is an issue that has been raised about protecting our democracy from foreign interference, and the government is taking action on that,” she told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.

Reform’s economy spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said the two donors were well aware of the law. He said: “It’s a breakthrough moment, really, for the party. It means that we will be battle ready if Andy Burnham calls an election, and we can compete now finally on a fair, even playing field with the two old parties.”

articles.title: Donald Trump doubles down on support for united Ireland
articles.summary:
US president says ‘many people agree’ with his view on unification, brushing off Andy Burnham’s opposition to referendum

Donald…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has reiterated his support for Irish unification and brushed off Andy Burnham’s opposition to a referendum. “Everybody says that. Then things happen,” the US president said on Sunday of the British prime minister’s response.
“It seems to me that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together,” Trump said of the unification of Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.

Trump caused consternation on both sides of the Irish Sea on Saturday when, at the start of a two-day visit to Ireland, he said he would “love” to see a united Ireland and “it may as well happen now”.

Downing Street said Burnham still believed there was not the required support for unification to trigger a referendum, as set out in the 1998 Good Friday peace agreement. Two weeks ago, Burnham said a referendum was “off the table”.
Irish nationalists welcomed Trump’s remarks, while the Conservative party and Northern Irish unionists condemned them.

blocks.caption: The Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin Donald speaks to reporters at the Irish open, at Trump International Golf Links and Hotel in Doonbeg, Co Clare. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA

blocks.text: On Sunday Trump expressed delight at the controversy. “Many people agree. I made what I considered to be a fairly routine comment, I have had so much support on that,” he said, speaking from Doonbeg, his county Clare golf resort that is hosting the Irish Open.
Asked about independence for Scotland, he reserved opinion. “I won’t talk about Scotland yet, I will save that.”
The leaders of Plaid Cymru, the Scottish National party and Sinn Féin are meeting in Cardiff on Monday, where they will discuss ways to strengthen cooperation for constitutional change.

Angela Rayner, the UK’s communities secretary, played down the president’s remarks. “Donald Trump is Donald Trump, and the president will say and speak his mind as he sees it,” she told Sky News. The government was serious about the Good Friday agreement and would “continue on that path”, she said.

Trump’s comments were awkward for the Irish government, which prefers to discuss cross-border initiatives rather than unification. Last month the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said that he “goes bananas” when his Fianna Fáil party colleagues call for a border poll.

On Sunday Martin said there had been “overreaction” to Trump’s comments. “He takes a different sort of perspective on things. We know that,” he said. “I think if everyone keeps a calm perspective on things, you know, we will take it from there.”

Sinn Féin figures welcomed Trump’s support for Irish unification. “They reflect the broad North American sentiment towards Irish unity and particularly the Irish diaspora towards Irish reunification,” said Gerry Adams, the party’s former leader.
Adams accused successive Irish governments of being “incredibly shortsighted” and failing to plan for unification. “There is no excuse for this.”
Trump’s comments also proved awkward for Northern Ireland unionists who have supported the president on other topics.

“Everyone is allowed a personal opinion even when it’s wrong,” said Ian Paisley Jr, a former Democratic Unionist party MP. “The political, cultural and economic reality is that Northern Ireland and its people are British and wish to remain so,” he said.

articles.title: Dawson College shooting survivor turned police officer reflects on friend's death 20 years on

image.caption: Former Dawson College students and survivors James Santos, centre, Meaghan Hennegan, left and Hayder Kadhim attend a ceremony commemorating the 20th anniversary of the shooting in which one person was killed and 19 others wounded, in Montreal on Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadia

blocks.text: Warning: The story below contains details about the moments leading up to the death of Anastasia De Sousa.
Two decades ago, James Santos saw his friend die in a shooting at a Montreal college. Now he is a Montreal police officer working for the force he says saved his life that day.
Sunday marks the 20th anniversary of the shooting.
On Sept. 13, 2006, a gunman entered Dawson College and opened fire on students in the hall. He killed 18-year-old Anastasia De Sousa and injured 19 others.

Santos, then a 17-year-old student, was having lunch with De Sousa that day. The cafeteria was packed and the two found a free table close to the entrance, he recalled in an interview with The Canadian Press.
“We were talking about our weekend and what we did and we had laughs — and then, all of a sudden, I see the shooter walk in,” he said.
When he realized the man had a real weapon, Santos dove behind some chairs. De Sousa, who couldn’t see the shooter, stood up.
“She turned around facing the shooter and basically one of the first shots was directed to my friend,” recalled Santos.
Thinking De Sousa fainted, Santos crawled over to drag her to cover.
“That's when I realized she got hit by one of the rounds near the abdomen. So I tried to console her, tell her that I was next to her and that everything will be alright,” he said.
Soon, the shooter turned his attention back to Santos. He told Santos to get up and get in front of him, essentially acting as a human shield. Santos obeyed.
“I didn't want to anger him because I believed that Anastasia was still there, and I also had other friends that were trapped,” he said.
He tried to talk the shooter down. At that moment, Santos recalled, he accepted that he would die.
“I just didn't want to take other students with me,” he said.
Her daughter was killed in the Dawson shooting. After 20 years, she still lives with the what-ifs
He fed the shooter white lies about the layout of the school, telling him one corridor led to a janitor’s closet or that another led nowhere.
When the shooter asked Santos how De Sousa was doing, Santos didn’t know what to say.
At that point, he still hoped his friend was alive. So he told the shooter that he wasn’t sure and asked him to let him get her help.

“He didn't say anything — he just loaded his magazine into a semi automatic and walked over to her, he unloaded all his 12 rounds on her, and then he came back and he told me, ‘Well, now you have nothing to worry about,’” said Santos.
Santos froze. Later, when the shooter held another student at gunpoint, Santos snapped, yelling at the shooter to leave the student be.
“I think I had enough with everything. Enough with the gunshots, the blood, the screaming of the students, just all of it," said Santos.
"The shooter didn't say anything, he just laughed.”
The shooter spared that other student. Moments later, police shot him in the leg. Santos was sure the angered gunman would shoot him. Instead, the shooter killed himself.

items: 'Why did you go to school that day?': Mother of Dawson shooting victim reflects 20 years later

blocks.text: Santos ran off. He thought it had been hours since De Sousa was killed and the ordeal began.
“I found out a little later on that it was a dozen minutes that passed by,” he said.
In 2008, then-Governor General of Canada Michaëlle Jean awarded Santos the Star of Courage for his actions that day.

Dawson College commemorated the shooting on Friday in a ceremony that brought De Sousa's family, survivors and students together in the school's Peace Garden. Loved ones remembered De Sousa's cheerful and resilient character.
During the ceremony, De Sousa's mother, Louise De Sousa, called on the federal government to tighten gun control laws.
Santos said the journey to becoming an officer was a challenging one, as he worked over years to overcome the trauma.
Talking about the events of that day two decades later, Santos seems calm, his voice never wavering.
“I have all the details in my mind. I recall everything, but I don't put myself into it. I'm looking at it as a third person,” he said.
That wasn’t always the case, he said.
“Initially, saying it the first couple of times was extremely, extremely, extremely hard. There's really no words to place it, just because you pretty much relive every second of it,” he said.

items: 'Why did I make it?': Survivors of Dawson shooting on compassion, finding purpose

blocks.text: Nonetheless, as he tells the story, little details come up. The way De Sousa had wanted to go out for lunch, but Santos instead opted to eat at the cafeteria. The fact that she sat with her back to the door and couldn’t see the shooter coming in.
Santos said he fixated on some of these details after graduating from Dawson, filled with survivor’s guilt.
“What if I had given her the [other] chair?" he asked.
"It just goes down that spiral that it's extremely hard to get out because you could think of anything, but it'll never change what actually happened."
He had considered a career in law enforcement before the event of 2006, and he said his experience during the shooting pushed him to want to join the Montreal police.
“I wanted to give back to the community that gave me another chance, right? The police [officers] gave me another chance at life.”

The path to get there wasn’t easy. Santos had vivid nightmares and panic attacks, and he knew he would have to address his trauma if he wanted to work as a police officer. He turned to therapy and set small goals, like watching an action movie, or one with a lot of shooting, until he could get through it calmly.
Then he joined the army. Training was a challenge, he said.
“The smell of gunpowder would bring me right back to the event of Dawson,” he said.
After about a decade in the military, Santos got into the police academy. He then worked for a year in a town outside of Montreal before joining the Montreal force in 2018.

“As a police officer, you never know what calls you're getting. [If] I get a call, I'm not going to be having anxiety or sweating or anything, because of all the little things I did prior to get myself to where I am today,” he said.

articles.title: Trump downplays AI risks after dire expert warnings and calls to slow development down
articles.summary: The US President said "negative forces" were airing concerns about "things that won't happen".

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has downplayed risks posed by artificial intelligence following days of dire warnings by experts.
"You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up and they're bringing up things that won't happen," Trump said during a visit to Ireland.
One of the warnings came from a former Anthropic researcher who said "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued.

On Saturday, top industry bosses agreed and called for a slow-down. Trump did not directly address the idea, but said: "We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."
Trump spoke on the same day AI researcher Jacob Coxon - who quit Anthropic a few days ago - told the BBC staff who were developing the systems were "genuinely frightened" for the future of humanity.
Coxon – who has also worked at OpenAI – welcomed the idea of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China.

On Saturday, Elon Musk, owner of xAI, and Sam Altman of OpenAI, backed a warning from the head of Anthropic Dario Amodei that the pace of development should be slowed "to reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong".
The Anthropic CEO said any slowdown would have to be limited to avoid allowing China to pull ahead.
The issues surrounding AI have prompted fierce debate - and present a dilemma for many world leaders.
On one hand, the sector is seen as huge opportunity to boost economic growth and a way to improve outdated digital systems and ways of working.
But there have also been a number of incidents where AI appears to have gone seriously wrong.
In August OpenAI said it had slowed down training some of its most advanced AI models to improve security.
The ChatGPT-maker said it was adding new measures after its AI agents bypassed safeguards and hacked the tech start-up Hugging Face.
And the same month it was disclosed two of the world's most powerful AI tools created fake human profiles to try and trick people in attempted cyber-attacks.

The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) said in the most serious case, Anthropic's Mythos AI tried to gain access to a service by sending private messages, having set up fake accounts mimicking real people - then hid the evidence.

articles.title: Russia struck train near Poland border shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials passed through
articles.summary: The former UK PM said "I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning".

blocks.text: A Russian strike has hit a train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other top European officials had passed through.
No casualties were reported after the Russian strike, which hit the train's engine.
Johnson and some of Europe's most senior security advisers, including the UK's Jonathan Powell, had passed along the same line on their way back from a conference in the capital, Kyiv.

Russia said Sunday it struck "railway infrastructure" in western Ukraine, but the former PM said "I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning" and asked "When are we going to give them the air defences they need?"
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a Russian drone had struck 800m from Polish border.
Russia has in recent months carried out a number of deadly attacks targeting Ukraine's trains, railway depots and other transport facilities.
Earlier this month, six employees of the state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia were killed after a depot was hit in Kyiv.
This week, a female conductor died in a Russian drone attack on a passenger train in southern Ukraine.
In January, President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned as "terrorism" a Russian strike on a crowded passenger train in the north-eastern Kharkiv region that left five people dead.

The Russian attacks have significantly damaged Ukraine's vast train network - the main mode of transportation for millions of Ukrainians as all air travel has been suspended since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

articles.title: ‘Biased impeach vote likely for absent senator-judges’
articles.summary: Senator-judges who missed the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte might end up voting based solely on political persuasion or alliances, Sen. Panfilo Lacson warned yesterday,…

blocks.text: September 14, 2026 | 12:00am
Senate opens impeachment court to public, but limits use of devices Senators start the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte at the Senate in Pasay, Metro Manila on July 6, 2026.
Aaron Favila, pool via AFP

MANILA, Philippines — Senator-judges who missed the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte might end up voting based solely on political persuasion or alliances, Sen. Panfilo Lacson warned yesterday, questioning how absent members can make an informed decision to convict or acquit the impeached official.
In an interview over radio dzBB, Lacson voiced concerns that colleagues who failed to hear testimony and observe witness demeanor throughout the trial could compromise fairness.
“How can they decide now? They will just rely on their political persuasion or political alliance,” he said.

Lacson raised the issue as the impeachment court prepares to consult with four amici curiae (friends of the court): retired chief justices Artemio Panganiban, Reynato Puno and Hilario Davide Jr., and retired Supreme Court associate justice Adolfo Azcuna, regarding the required voting threshold for conviction.
The legal experts were invited after presiding officer Francis Escudero consulted the prosecution and defense panels.
Senator-judges are expected to vote on Sen. Erwin Tulfo’s motion for reconsideration regarding the 16-vote, or two-thirds threshold previously ruled on by Escudero.
Lacson cautioned the Senate against intervening in the petitions of detained Senators Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada to participate in the trial.
Marcoleta has written to Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and Escudero seeking permission to vote, while Estrada’s bid to attend was rejected by the Sandiganbayan in July.
Bato, Loren
Asked about Sen. Ronald dela Rosa, Lacson distinguished between members who never took the oath as judges and those who did but missed proceedings.
Dela Rosa has been in hiding following the issuance of an arrest warrant against him by the International Criminal Court and after fleeing the Senate compound following a shooting incident on May 13.

Meanwhile, Sen. Loren Legarda has been abroad for several weeks now amid personal health issues and plunder allegations over P10.44 billion in incomplete solar energy projects awarded to her son, Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste.
Lacson said Legarda has reached out to colleagues for moral support.

articles.title: AMLC to confirm P6.7 billion bank transactions of VP, Mans?
articles.summary: The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) is expected to present to the Senate impeachment court today its report on the P6.7 billion in transactions linked to the bank accounts of Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: September 14, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte arrives before the start of the impeachment trial at the Senate of the Philippines in Pasay, Metro Manila on July 7, 2026.
Noel Celis, pool / AFP

MANILA, Philippines — The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) is expected to present to the Senate impeachment court today its report on the P6.7 billion in transactions linked to the bank accounts of Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio under Article II of the impeachment, on unexplained wealth.

The AMLC report was previously discussed during House proceedings on Duterte’s impeachment, with the figures cited including P6.7 billion in aggregate transactions and P4.4 billion in inflows involving the couple.

The figure represents aggregated transactions over the years and is not by itself equivalent to the couple’s net worth, making the underlying bank records important to establishing what the transactions actually represent.
Of the P6.7 billion, “inflows” amounted to P4.4 billion, while “outflows” totaled P1.5 billion.

Prosecutors have since obtained bank and tax records through subpoenas issued by the Senate impeachment court, giving them access to financial documents that were not available during the earlier House inquiry.

Additionally, the prosecution has lined up retired Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang, ombudsman records division officer-in-charge Karen Batu and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) company registration and monitoring department director Gerardo del Rosario among its witnesses today.
Akbayan party-list Rep. Chel Diokno will be the prosecutor in charge of Article II.

Cabotaje-Tang is expected to testify on principles governing public accountability and integrity in public office, including mechanisms for addressing undisclosed or unexplained wealth and prohibited business interests.

Batu will testify on Duterte’s statement of assets, liabilities and net worth in the custody of the Office of the Ombudsman, while Del Rosario is expected to identify and authenticate SEC records involving companies and business interests linked to Duterte and Carpio.
Article II accuses Duterte of betrayal of public trust for allegedly accumulating wealth disproportionate to her lawful income and failing to fully and truthfully disclose her assets and liabilities.

Earlier, Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon, one of the House prosecutors who will be helping Diokno in Article II, said the prosecution was completing preparations for both its documentary and testimonial evidence.
The prosecution is preparing more than 1,800 bank, tax and other financial documents for Article II, including records involving Duterte, Carpio and companies linked to them.
Ridon had described bank and Bureau of Internal Revenue records obtained by the prosecution as the “last important pillar” of its evidence on Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.

Prosecutors plan to examine the financial records alongside Duterte’s SALNs and information from the AMLC to determine whether her assets and financial transactions can be reconciled with her declared wealth and legitimate sources of income.
The prosecution has also served Duterte with 104 requests for admission involving subpoenaed bank records and the ownership of accounts identified in them.
Commenting on the impeachment case and criminal complaint for grave threats filed at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court, Ridon said Duterte only has herself to blame.

As far as Ridon is concerned, Duterte’s open threat to have President Marcos, First Lady Liza Marcos and former speaker Martin Romualdez killed was the original sin that resulted in her cases today, adding she should stop insinuating political motivations for her problems.

articles.title: House plenary debates on 2027 budget begin this week
articles.summary: Plenary deliberations on the P7.2-trillion national budget will start this week at the House of Representatives, as lawmakers try to finish the government’s spending bill before the…

blocks.text: September 14, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Plenary deliberations on the P7.2-trillion national budget will start this week at the House of Representatives, as lawmakers try to finish the government’s spending bill before the congressional recess next month and until after the Undas break.
Sponsorship and plenary debates on the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB) will start Tuesday and are expected to be finished on Sept. 25.

The Development Budget Coordination Committee led by the Department of Budget and Management and Department of Finance, in coordination with the Department of Economy, Planning and Development, Office of the President and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas submitted the 2027 National Expenditure Plan to the House last Aug. 11.

Under the House’s schedule of activities, second reading of the 2027 GAB is slated on Oct. 6 to be followed by the third reading on Oct. 9, after which it will be transmitted to the Senate on the same day.

House appropriations committee chair Mikaela Suansing and Speaker Faustino Dy III said the chamber is on track with its timeline in passing the 2027 GAB, with Dy assuring taxpayers that they will scrutinize every centavo in the budget for 2027 to ensure public funds are properly allocated.

Speaking at a press briefing over the weekend in a public consultation in South Cotabato, Dy said the national budget is currently the most important measure being tackled by the House because of its direct impact on communities and families across the country.
DepEd budget augmentation

Sibling Reps. Migz and Luigi Villafuerte of the 5th and 2nd districts of Camarines Sur, respectively, are pushing for the augmentation of the Department of Education’s P975.9-billion budget for 2027 by adding P12 billion more for the career growth program of teachers and school heads.
In separate statements, they underscored the need for this year’s promotion of more than 5,000 public school teachers and school heads in the province alone.

articles.title: Palace: Indian firms to expand in Philippines
articles.summary: Several Indian firms committed to expand their operations in the Philippines, including on agricultural technology, health care and digital infrastructure during their meeting with President Marcos…

blocks.text: September 14, 2026 | 12:00am
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. arrives at New Delhi, India on September 12, 2026 to attend the 18th BRICS Summit where he will represent the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
Photo / Presidential Communications Office

MANILA, Philippines — Several Indian firms committed to expand their operations in the Philippines, including on agricultural technology, health care and digital infrastructure during their meeting with President Marcos in New Delhi, India on Saturday.

In a statement yesterday, the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said Marcos met with iSON Group, a New Delhi-based conglomerate with businesses in agrotechnology, health care, telecommunications, information technology, renewable energy, business process outsourcing (BPO) and insurance.
According to Trade Secretary Cristina Roque, iSON Group discussed expansion plans in three key areas: agricultural technology, health care, and BPO and digital infrastructure.
The group has committed $75 million in new and scaled-up investments in the Philippines, which is expected to generate around 2,000 jobs, PCO said.
The investments include a proposed $50-million agro-solar project, health care and 24/7 teleconsultation services, and a $10-million expansion in BPO and global delivery centers.?
Roque said the proposed teleconsultation service could help address health care access challenges in remote communities.
The proposed service would cost around P65 per month and allow patients to consult doctors at any time, subject to the company’s final implementation plans.?
“This is very helpful for us, especially in areas where access to doctors and health care facilities remains limited,” Roque said.??

With more than 25,000 employees and operations in around 35 countries, iSON Group through its digital infrastructure arm iSON Tower Ltd. Inc., has operated in the Philippines since 2021 under the Department of Information and Communications Technology’s Common Tower Policy.
The company has deployed around $65 million to build 450 telecommunications towers serving approximately 600 tenants across Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao.

Marcos also met with NPCI International Ltd. to advance cooperation on digital payments, including a partnership with LandBank to explore the adoption in the Philippines of a payment system based on India’s Unified Payments Interface.
The initiative could make government payments more efficient, improve interoperability of QR-based payments, and facilitate faster cross-border transactions.

The President likewise met with executives of GMR Group and representatives of Cavitex Holdings Inc. to advance the development of the Sangley Point International Airport project – a world-class, multi-runway aviation hub that will help decongest the Ninoy Aquino International Airport.

Marcos also led an executive roundtable discussion with executives of Cognizant, VVDN Technologies, Hinduja Group and HCLTech, which already have operations or a presence in the Philippines.?Roque said the four companies indicated plans to expand in digitalization, AI, telecommunications and other technology-driven industries.??
Also present during the meetings were Finance Secretary Frederick Go, Information and Communications Technology Secretary Henry Aguda and other senior officials from the Philippine government.?
Marcos was in India to attend the 18th BRICS Summit on Sunday in his capacity as this year’s chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
He was also expected to hold a bilateral meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

articles.title: Gibo to reserve force: Protect Philippines land, maritime domain
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. has called on the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Reserve Force to help protect the country’s maritime domain.

blocks.text: September 14, 2026 | 12:00am
Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.
Department of National Defense - Philippines / Facebook page
MANILA, Philippines — Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. has called on the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Reserve Force to help protect the country’s maritime domain.

Teodoro made the call during the culmination of the 47th AFP National Reservist Week at Camp Aguinaldo on Saturday as he highlighted the Reserve Force’s role in addressing gaps in the AFP’s active duty force structure through “force and mission replication and support,” including “functional replication, and substitution, if necessary, of operating units.”

He asked the Reserve Force to pursue activities along the Pacific Ocean boundary and areas leading to the Pacific Ocean, particularly in coastal and island provinces, where the country faces vulnerabilities in its eastern seaboard.

“Our vulnerability is in the eastern seaboard. I would like the Reserve Commands to pursue activities on our Pacific Ocean boundary and or areas leading to the Pacific Ocean. That is a huge gap,” Teodoro said.

As a maritime and archipelagic country, he said the Philippines must control its territorial land domain, baseline areas from which its maritime entitlements are drawn, its exclusive economic zone (EEZ), and other areas under its jurisdiction, including its extended continental shelves.

He emphasized the country’s responsibility to help secure supply chains and protect Filipino seafarers, whom he identified as the number one nationality victimized by piracy and other untoward activities due to world and ethnic conflicts elsewhere.
He identified three major threats confronting the country according to their imminence: natural calamities and disasters, internal and external security threats, and actual conflict.

For internal and external security threats, he emphasized deterrence as the country’s prime objective, requiring increased posture through infrastructure, capabilities, force size, and activities conducted singly, bilaterally, or multilaterally to demonstrate the ability to resist threats.

Teodoro emphasized the need for continued modernization, infrastructure build-up, enhancing community survivability, and internal hardening against malign foreign influence and disinformation, noting the reality of cognitive warfare and changing narratives.

articles.title: Pregnant woman among more than 10 killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza
articles.summary:
Woman’s family says she died of injuries after being shot in the head while sitting inside a tent near Khan Younis

A pregnant Palestinian woman died on Saturday from injuries sustained after…
articles.byline: Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem and Seham Tantesh in Gaza

blocks.text: A pregnant Palestinian woman died on Saturday from injuries sustained after being shot in the head by Israeli forces south of Khan Younis, according to her family and medical workers, as strikes across Gaza killed at least 10 people in 48 hours.

The woman, named as Iman Shalouf, 27, who was nearly eight months pregnant, was sitting inside her family’s tent in the al-Mawasi area when Israeli gunfire struck her, according to paramedics and witnesses.

‘‘We heard the sound of gunfire while I was praying,’’ Wathfa abu Mashi, Shalouf’s mother-in-law, said in a video interview with Anadolu. “My daughter asked me, ‘Where is Iman?’ I told her she was in her tent. She went to check on her and found her covered in blood after she was hit by a bullet.”
Shalouf’s husband, Ismail abu Mashi, said “Where is the ceasefire they keep talking about? There is no such thing. There is killing every day. People are dying here every day.”
Shalouf was rushed to Nasser hospital, where doctors initially detected her unborn baby’s heartbeat, but she and her unborn baby died a few hours later.
According to relatives, Shalouf had already chosen the name Ayoub for the baby, who was due in November.
Relatives and community members gathered at the hospital to hold funeral prayers for Shalouf and her child before carrying their bodies for burial in Khan Younis. They were buried side by side.
Contacted by the Guardian, the Israel Defense Forces said they were looking into the incident.
Despite the ceasefire agreement reached in October 2025, violence and the killing of Palestinians continue on a daily basis.

The health ministry in Gaza said 10 Palestinians had been killed and 56 wounded in Israeli attacks over the previous 48 hours, amid artillery shelling and gunfire in several areas of northern, central and southern Gaza.

blocks.caption: Displaced Palestinians walk among the ruins of buildings in al-Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood east of Gaza City. Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPA

blocks.text: Four members of the same family – Momen Ahmed, his wife, Haneen Saleh, and their daughters Lana, 12, and Bana, eight – were killed when their home in Beit Lahiya was struck on Thursday night, according to the ministry. Six other Palestinians were reported killed in Khan Younis and Gaza City on Friday, including a man who died of wounds sustained in an earlier attack.

Several other Palestinians were injured in attacks across Gaza. On Friday, two people were reportedly seriously injured in an attack in Beit Lahiya, while three people including a woman six months pregnant and a child were wounded by gunfire in the same city.
On Saturday, nine people were injured when a displaced people’s tent in al-Mawasi was shelled, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent.

On Sunday, two Palestinians were killed and several others injured when a vehicle was struck in Tel al-Hawa in Gaza City, according to the health ministry. The attack also injured people on a passing bus carrying women and children.

On 28 August, Unicef said at least four children had been reported killed in the preceding five days and many others wounded, including children who sustained life-changing injuries. On 2 September, it said three other children had reportedly been killed and at least five others injured in the preceding 24 hours, bringing the number of children reportedly killed between 23 August and 2 September to seven.

“Airstrikes by Israeli forces continue killing and wounding Palestinians,” Médecins Sans Frontières said. “Between September 6 and 9, Israeli forces issued 18 so-called evacuation orders and struck a building less than 250ft from an MSF clinic.”

The humanitarian situation remains severe. According to the UN’s humanitarian office, “most of Gaza’s 2.1 million are approaching the rainy season in overcrowded displacement sites, at risk of flooding and disease, while efforts to help them prepare are constrained by funding shortfalls and access restrictions”.
On 31 August, a temporary halt to desalination in Israel reduced the water available to about a million people in Gaza who rely on the Israeli grid.
Several electricity generators at hospitals across the Gaza Strip have stopped working because of shortages of spare parts and fuel, the territory’s health ministry has said.

According to the ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025. Since Israel’s war in Gaza began on 7 October 2023, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the ministry.

articles.title: From wards to the presidential suite: Room rates at the PGH
articles.summary: The PGH is a tertiary state-owned hospital located in Manila. Primarily funded through the UP System's budget allocation, it offers several types of rooms.

blocks.text: Published September 13, 2026 11:51pm

A few days after former House Speaker Martin Romualdez was arrested in his hospital bed at a private hospital, the Sandiganbayan ordered his transfer to the Philippine General Hospital (PGH) to verify his doctors' medical findings.

The PGH is a tertiary state-owned hospital located in Manila. It is administered and operated by the University of the Philippines Manila and is primarily funded through the UP System's budget allocation.
Romualdez was moved to the PGH on Saturday, entering through what the hospital's guards said was not the regular entryway for patients.
It has not been disclosed what room the former Speaker is in, but according to its website, PGH offers at least 10 types of rooms under its Department of Private Patient Services (DPPS).
The most affordable option is the “Ward” at a daily rate of P715, followed by “Semi-Private I” (one to three beds) at P1,000 per day, and the “Cubicle” at P1,100.
“Semi-Private II” rooms accommodate one to two beds and are priced at P1,430 daily. The final option priced below two thousand pesos is the “Studio Room” at P1,650 per day.

PGH also offers “Small Private” and “Big Private” rooms at P2,200 and P2,750, respectively, while “Superior” rooms are priced at P3,300. The PGH's 2026 Citizen’s Charter lists the price for a Big Private room at P1,500.
The two most expensive options under the DPPS are the Executive Room at P5,500 per day and the Presidential Suite, which costs P6,600 per day.

The room rates provided by PGH cover only the base daily accommodation charge and do not include additional hospital expenses such as professional fees, laboratory tests, and other medical procedures. — BM, GMA News
